units.la: ILLVSTRISSIMI PRINCIPES ac Domini, Religionis verae in sinceritate ac pace conservationem non tantum ad muneris vestri cu-ram pertinere, sed etiam Reipublicae vestrae præci-puum esse στύλον[?] καὶ ἑδραίωμα, optimè Vos intelligere reipsa ostenditis. Conservari veram Religionem in sinceritate ac pace vix posse, in hac perversitatis humanæ malitiâ, prudens ac veneranda judicavit Antiquitas, nisi extent in Ecclesiis publicæ consensus in doctrinâ orthodoxâ Formulæ, seu breves & dilucidæ pr[?]incipuorum[?] Fidei Articulorum ex verbo DEI declarationes, communi[?] Ecclesiarum consilio & consensu institutæ, quarum approbatione omnes Ecclesiarum doctores consensum suum in doctrinâ orthodoxâ, ejusque traditione, testatum faciant. Habitum hoc semper fuit, jam inde ab Apostolorum temporibus, ad puritatem doctrinæ in Ecclesiis conservandam, nec non ad pacem ac concordiam in iisdem stabiliendam, commodissimum medium, atque etiam adversus hæreses & schismata expeditissimum remedium. Servivit olim huic fini in ipsis Christianæ Ecclesiæ primordiis Symbolum, quod vocatur Apostolorum, vel ab ipsis Apostolis, vel ab ipsorum Discipulis, viris Apostolicis, Ecclesiæ traditum, & per manus ad nos usque propagatum. Postmodùm quum varia in ipsis Ecclesiæ visceribus exorirentur hæreses, earumque autores ἐν πανουργίᾳ περιπατοῦντες[?], καὶ τὸν λόγον τῷ Θεῷ δολοῦντες, ad obtegendas corruptelas suas, ejusdem brevitate abuterentur, coactæ fuerunt Ecclesiæ orthodoxæ ejusdem prolixiorem ex verbo DEI repetitionem ac declarationem instituere, ut veritas tas cœlestis clariùs illustrari, & fraudulenta omnis hominum hæreticorum [?] detegi, præcaveri, atque ab Ecclesijs arceri queat. Factum hoc fuit communi Ecclesiarum consilio, Niceæ, Constantinopoli, Ephesi, Chalcedone, aliisque in locis, diversis temporibus, quotiescunque exorientium subinde hæreticorum improbitas hanc Ecclesijs necessitatem imposuit. Postulant enim omninò salus atque ædificatio Ecclesiæ, ut excitatæ controversiæ communi Ecclesiarum consilio examinentur, ac decidantur: utque earundem communi consensione propriæ quædam, perspicuæ, & genuino S. Scripturæ sensui congruentes explicationes, & loquendi formæ, constituantur, ne novis quotidie opinionibus ac locutionibus Ecclesiæ turbentur, aut distrahantur. Sinceritas doctrinæ, & pax Ecclesiarum conservari nequaquam possunt, nisi hac ratione novaturientium licentia coërceatur, & hæreticorum fraudibus, quibus in Ecclesias irrepere solent, occurratur. Imprimis necesse habuerunt Ecclesiæ, quæ per singularem DEI gratiam ab erroribus, superstitionibus, atque idololatriâ, quibus Antichristus ille magnus Ecclesiam Christianam miserandum in modum conspurcavit, repurgatæ ex Babylone illâ profugerunt, publicâ atque apertâ veritaveritatis Evangelicæ, quam amplectuntur con-sessione fidei suæ, quam profitentur, atque etiam justissimæ suæ à Papatu discessionis rationem reddere, calumniis improborum obviam ire, consensum in doctrina cum reliquis Ecclesijs Reformatis testari, & posteris fidei suæ testimonium relinquere. Quare uti reliquæ nationum omnium Ecclesiæ Reformatæ suas fidei Confessiones has ob causas ediderunt, ita quoque Majores nostri, qui Ecclesias hasce Reformatas per Belgium, plerique etiam sanguine suo, fundarunt, hanc quoque Fidei & Doctrinæ suæ, ob cujus professionem gravissimas ab Hispanica crudelitate persecutiones sustinebant, Confessionem publicam exstare voluerunt. Hujus-modi Confessiones quia conscriptæ sunt ab hominibus qui errare potuerunt, non sunt, nec esse possunt, autoritatis αὐτοπίστως [?] καὶ αὐτεξούσιος [?] (hæc enim prærogativa soli Sacræ & Θεοπνεύστῳ [?] Scripturæ competit) ad normam verbi divini semper expendi debent, si quis in ijs errorem se posse ostendere existimet. Hanc tamen in Ecclesijs autoritatem obtinere debent, ut habeantur pro publicis receptæ in Ecclesijs doctrinæ, doctorumque in eâdem consensus Formulis, ac pro sententijs, quæ communi Ecclesiarum approbatione verbo DEI consentire judijudicantur : quibus proinde debeant subscribere omnes, qui in Ecclesiis illis publico docendi munere fungi volent. Nec unquam permittendum est, ut qui semel Confessioni publicæ subscripsit, autoritate privatâ quidquam in eâ immutet, aut diversum ab eâ doceat. Fieri enim non potest, quin statim contentiones & schismata in Ecclesiis inde exoriantur. Cæterum si quis existimet se in recepta doctrina aliquid observasse, quod sacris literis minus consentaneum arbitretur, communi Ecclesiarum judicio expendendum proponere debet, ut si rationes eius verbo divino congruere comperiantur, communi consilio mutatio instituatur : sin minus, ut aut Ecclesiæ judicio acquiescat, aut desinat docere in illis Ecclesiis, quarum doctrinam ipse non approbet. Hæc usitata ac commodissima ratio est Ecclesias à contentionibus & schismatibus in pace conservandi. Atque hac ratione Ecclesiæ nostræ altam pacem atque amabilem concordiam inter se coluerunt, tam sub crudelissimis persecutionibus, quam postea cum Vos, Illustrissimi Principes ac Domini, altores & vindices natæ sunt, sub gravissimo bello, per annos plus minus quinquaginta. Tentarunt quidem nonnulli, qui vetus Papismi fermentum penitus non expurgaverant, paucis in locus quædam innovare, & suavem hanc Ecclesiarum harmoniam aisturbare, sed imperita istorum audacia legitimis Ecclesiarum nostrarum censuris, & autoritate vestrâ maturè repressa fuit. Donec tandem incidimus in infœlices & pernitiosissimas hasce contentiones ac controversias, quibus statut non tantum Ecclesiarum, sed & Reipubl. miserè concussus, conturbatus & tantum non eversus fuit. Caussam earum omnes prudentes norunt aliam non fuisse, quam quod nonnulli Ecclesiarum nostrarum Doctores, qui in doctrinâ receptâ quædam desiderare videbantur, viam[?] hanc regiam ingredi noluerint, sed opiniones suas discrepantes contra laudabilem Ecclesiarum ordinem atque u-sum, antequam cum Ecclesiis rationes suas commu-nicassent, aut Ecclesiæ de illis legitimè cognoscere & judicare potuerint, in vulgus publicè & priva-tim, concionibus & scriptis suis, sparserint: quin etiam impediverint hactenus tantis viribus, ne legitima aliqua cognitio Ecclesiastica de iis instituere-tur. Huic malo ut tandem aliquando remedium adhibeatur idoneum, laudandum est omnibus mo-dis, Illustrissimi Principes ac Domini, decretum vestrum, quo, exemplo piorum principum Chri-stianorum, ex usu Ecclesiarum Reformatarum, atque etiam ex consilio saluberrimo Serenissimi Magnæ Britanniæ Regis, statuistis, ut de Controversijs hisce nostris in legitima Synodo Nationali harum Ecclesiarum cognoscatur, & legitimum examen ac judicium secundum divini verbi normam instituatur. Ordinarium hoc semper fuit in Ecclesiâ DEI adversus istiusmodi mala remedium, maximo cum pacis & veritatis emolumento à Christianis principibus sæpè adhibitum. Ad hanc Synodum quia prudentissimè judicastis operæpretium fore doctissimos quosque & veritatis ac pacis amantissimos Theologos ex vicinis Regnis & Rebuspublicis invitari, ut tanti momenti negotium quasi communi omnium Reformatarum Ecclesiarum consilio maturius expendi, & accuratius componi queat, existimavi me illis & toti Synodo utilem navaturum operam, si specimen aliquot Controversiarum, quibus Ecclesiæ nostræ hactenus sunt turbatæ, Latinè exhiberem, ut ex eo aliquâ ex parte cognoscant, quibus de controversijs in hac Synodo potissimùm erit agendum. Ad tollendas enim Controversias, imprimis necessarium est, statum earum sollicitè inquiri, & rectè formari, ut deinceps expensis accuratè in timore DEI utriusque partis rationibus, eadem secundum verbi divini normam debitè decidantur: Adjunxi etiam harmoniam Ca-nonum Ecclesiasticorū in superioribus Synodis Na-tionalibus constitutorum, secundum quos hactenus Ecclesiarum nostrarum regimen fuit institutum: ut hac ratione exteri Theologi ad Synodum hanc ven-turi de controversijs, Doctrinâ, & Regimine Eccle-siarum, quasi compendio erudiri queant. Hunc la-borem meum si Vobis, Illustrissimi Principes & Do-mini, non displicere intellexero, est quod serio mihi gratuler. Suscep-tum fuisse eo tantum animo, ut Ec-clesijs nostris patrijs prodesset, novit ille ὁ περιπατῶν [?] ἐν μέσῳ τ λυχνιῶν τ χρυσῶν [?], quem supplex veneror, ut in futura hac Synodo Nationali, quae quasi Genera-lis haberi merito poterit, Spiritu suo Sancto praesi-deat, eámque ita moderetur, ut per ipsam Ecclesijs nostris pristina pax restituatur, Doctrina orthodoxa in illis magis magisque illustretur ac stabiliatur, & collapsum regimen restauretur, ad divinae gloriae pro-pagationem & subditorum vestrorum salutem. Im-primis etiam, ut Vos, Illustrissimi Principes & Do-mini, potenti dextera sua protegat, optimis consilijs vestris, ac toti gubernationi ubertim benedicat, atque incolumitatem Vobis longaevam concedat.
units.tr: MOST ILLUSTRIOUS LORDS and Masters, you show by your actions that you understand well that preserving the true religion in purity and peace belongs not only to the care of your office but is also the chief pillar and foundation [στύλον καὶ ἑδραίωμα] of your commonwealth. Antiquity judged, prudently and with reverence, that the true religion can hardly be preserved in purity and peace in this wickedness of human perversity, unless the Churches possess a public consensus in orthodox doctrine, that is, formularies, brief and clear declarations of the chief articles of faith drawn from the Word of God, established by the common counsel and agreement of the Churches, by whose approval all the teachers of the Churches may attest their agreement in orthodox doctrine and its tradition. From the very beginnings of the Apostles, this has always been the most convenient means of keeping doctrine pure in the Churches, of establishing peace and concord among them, and also the most effective remedy against heresies and schisms. In the earliest days of the Christian Church, the creed called the Apostles' served this purpose; it was handed down by the Apostles themselves or by their disciples, men of apostolic standing, and has been passed from hand to hand down to us. Later, when various heresies arose within the very bosom of the Church, and their authors, walking in craftiness and handling the word of God deceitfully [ἐν πανουργίᾳ περιπατοῦντες, καὶ τὸν λόγον τοῦ Θεοῦ δολοῦντες], abused the brevity of that creed to cover their corruptions, the orthodox Churches were compelled to draw up a fuller repetition and declaration of it from the Word of God, so that heavenly truth might be more clearly illustrated, and every fraud of heretics might be detected, guarded against, and kept out of the Churches. This was done by the common counsel of the Churches at Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, Chalcedon, and in other places, at various times, whenever the wickedness of heretics arising from time to time imposed this necessity on the Churches. For the safety and building up of the Church absolutely require that controversies which arise be examined and decided by the common counsel of the Churches, and that by their common consent certain proper, clear explanations and forms of speech, agreeing with the genuine sense of Holy Scripture, be established, so that the Churches are not daily disturbed or divided by new opinions and expressions. The purity of doctrine and the peace of the Churches cannot be preserved in any other way than by restraining the license of innovators and meeting the frauds of heretics, by which they are wont to creep into the Churches. Above all, the Churches which, by the singular grace of God, were cleansed from the errors, superstitions and idolatry with which that great Antichrist had miserably defiled the Christian Church, and which fled out of that Babylon, found it necessary to give a public and open confession of the truth of the Gospel, which they embrace, and a confession of their faith, which they profess; to give a reason for their most just departure from Popery; to meet the slanders of the wicked; to attest their agreement in doctrine with the other Reformed Churches; and to leave to posterity a testimony of their faith. Therefore, just as the Reformed Churches of all the nations have published their confessions of faith for these reasons, so also our forefathers, who founded these Reformed Churches throughout the Netherlands, many of them with their own blood, wished that a public confession of this faith and doctrine should exist, for the profession of which they endured the most grievous persecutions from Spanish cruelty. Since such confessions have been written by men who could err, they do not have, and cannot have, the authority of being self-certain and self-authoritative (for this prerogative belongs to Holy Scripture alone, which is God-breathed [θεόπνευστος]); they must always be weighed by the rule of the divine Word, if anyone thinks he can show an error in them. Nevertheless, they ought to have this authority in the Churches: that they be held as the public doctrine received in the Churches, and as formularies of the agreement of the teachers in it, and as opinions which by the common approval of the Churches are judged to agree with the Word of God. Therefore all who wish to hold the public office of teaching in those Churches ought to subscribe to them. Nor must it ever be permitted that one who has once subscribed the public confession should change anything in it by private authority, or teach anything different from it. For it cannot but be that quarrels and schisms arise in the Churches from this at once. If anyone thinks he has observed something in the received doctrine which he judges less consistent with the sacred letters, he ought to propose it for examination by the common judgment of the Churches, so that, if his reasons are found to agree with the divine Word, a change may be made by common counsel; but if not, that he either acquiesce in the judgment of the Church or cease to teach in those Churches whose doctrine he does not himself approve. This is the usual and most convenient way of keeping the Churches free from contentions and schisms and in peace. And by this method our Churches have cultivated a deep peace and lovely concord among themselves, both under the most cruel persecutions and afterwards, when they were born under your protection and defence, Most Illustrious Lords and Masters, in a most grievous war, for some fifty years. Indeed some, who had not thoroughly purged out the old leaven of Popery, tried in a few places to introduce novelties and to disturb this sweet harmony of the Churches; but the rash presumption of these men was promptly repressed by the lawful censures of our Churches and by your authority. Until at last we fell into these unhappy and most pernicious contentions and controversies, by which not only the Churches but also the commonwealth was wretchedly shaken, disturbed and almost overturned. All prudent people know that the cause of these was nothing other than that some teachers of our Churches, who seemed to desire certain changes in the received doctrine, were unwilling to enter upon this royal way, but, contrary to the praiseworthy order and custom of the Churches, before they had communicated their reasons with the Churches, or before the Churches could lawfully inquire into and judge them, spread their divergent opinions abroad publicly and privately, in sermons and in writings. Moreover, with such great efforts they have hitherto prevented any lawful ecclesiastical inquiry into them from being instituted. That a suitable remedy may at last be applied to this evil, it must be praised in every way, Most Illustrious Lords and Masters, that you have decreed, following the example of pious Christian princes, the practice of the Reformed Churches, and also the most wholesome counsel of the Most Serene King of Great Britain, that these our controversies be inquired into in a lawful National Synod of these Churches, and that a lawful examination and judgment be made according to the norm of the divine Word. This has always been the ordinary remedy in the Church of God against such evils, and has often been used by Christian princes with the greatest advantage to peace and truth. Since you have most prudently judged it worthwhile to invite to this Synod the most learned theologians who love truth and peace above all, from neighbouring kingdoms and commonwealths, so that a matter of such weight may be weighed more maturely and settled more accurately, as if by the common counsel of all the Reformed Churches, I thought that I would render a useful service both to them and to the whole Synod if I set out in Latin a sample of some of the controversies by which our Churches have hitherto been troubled, so that they may learn in some measure from it which controversies will chiefly have to be dealt with in this Synod. For to remove controversies, it is above all necessary to inquire carefully into their state and to frame it rightly, so that afterwards, when the reasons of both parties have been weighed accurately and in the fear of God, the matters may be duly decided according to the norm of the divine Word. I have also added a harmony of the ecclesiastical canons established in earlier National Synods, according to which the government of our Churches has hitherto been ordered, so that by this means foreign theologians coming to this Synod may be instructed, as it were in a summary, about the controversies, the doctrine and the government of the Churches. If I learn that this labour of mine does not displease you, Most Illustrious Lords and Masters, I shall have cause to congratulate myself sincerely. That it was undertaken with the sole purpose of benefiting our native Churches, He knows who walks in the midst of the seven golden candlesticks [ὁ περιπατῶν ἐν μέσῳ τῶν λυχνιῶν τῶν χρυσῶν], whom I humbly worship, that He would preside over this future National Synod, which may rightly be regarded as a kind of General Synod, with His Holy Spirit, and so guide it that through it the former peace may be restored to our Churches, orthodox doctrine may be more and more illustrated and established among them, and the fallen government may be restored, to the propagation of divine glory and the salvation of your subjects. Above all, may He protect you, Most Illustrious Lords and Masters, with His mighty right hand, bless abundantly your best counsels and the whole government, and grant you long life and well-being.

units.la: DE Controversijs, quæ in Reformatis, Ecclesijs Belgicis ante paucos annos excitatæ fuerunt, easdemq; Ecclesias miserè hactenus afflixerunt, varij apud exteros non solùm, sed domi quoq; sparguntur rumores. Qui infelicium harum Controversiarum autores sunt, ut facti tam intempestivi & noxij invidiam declinent, in eo toti nunc sunt, ut easdem omni ratione extenuent, persuadeántque omnibus litem tantùm ab ipsis moveri de quibusdam circa arduum illud de divinâ Prædestinatione dogma subti-litatibus, quæ ad promovendam hominum salutem neutiquam sint necessariæ. Prote-stantur publicè se præter quinque istos, ni-mis notos, de Prædestinatione, eiq; annexis capitibus, articulos, nihil habere, de quo contendant. Quod hæ controversiæ jam dudum sopitæ non sint, culpam omnem reji-ciunt in illos, qui ipsis adversantur, quoniam in articulis, uti prætendunt, ad salutem mi-nus necessarijs, dissentientes tolerare nolint. Alij rationes se habere putant gravissimas, quibus adducantur, vt non tantùm merito suspicentur, sed omninò etiam arbitrentur, plausibilem illam de Prædestinatione controversiam, quinq; illis Articulis expressam, πρόφασιν tantùm esse, sub quâ Socinianismum (aliquantulùm forte interpolatum aut incrustatum) in Reformatas hasce Ecclesias introducere conentur. Idq; eo magis credunt, quod ex scriptis etiam eorum qui protestationem illam manibus suis obsignarunt, ostendere clarissimè possint in multò pluribus articulis illos à receptâ harum Ecclesiarum doctrinâ discedere, atque ad errores Socinianorum accedere: quod etiam nullâ hactenus ratione permoveri potuerint, ut aperta ac rotundâ declaratione publicè testatum facerent, quid de præcipuis doctrinæ Reformatæ capitibus sentiant, aut quam procul à Socinianorum erroribus absint: quod denique ipsi profiteantur hasce ad promotionem causæ suæ artes adhiberi, ut apud vulgus non ulterius progrediantur, quam de Articulis vulgò notis: ut pro ingeniorum diversitate quosdam lacte diu alant, alijs solidiorem cibum maturius præbeant, alios rectà & aperte, alios per cunicucuniculos aggrediantur : cum quibusdam agant plane, & nihil dissimulate, seu quod ajunt, rotundâ phrasi, apud alios autem receptas loquendi formulas, adhibita commodâ interpretatione in bonum sensum trahant, ut vel nescientes verum discant, nec novitatis specie ab ipso limine repellantur. Adeò ut circa hasce Controversias tam de earundem statu, quam de veritate hodie concertetur. Quid de eo sit, brevi, volente Deo, Synodus Ecclesiarum Belgicarum Nationalis, ad examinandas tollendásque hasce Controversias ab Illustr. & Præpotent. ORDINIBVS GENERALIBVS convocata, despiciet & judicabit. Huic me rem nec ingratam nec inutilem facturum judicavi, si ea, quæ aliquando in usum meum privatum ex publicis doctorum Ecclesiarum nostrarum scriptis annotavi, in quibus à receptâ atque in Confessione Ecclesiarum nostrarum expressâ doctrinâ discedere videbantur, publicè communicarem. Descripsi omnia fide optimâ, uti virum bonum decet: de eo si quis forte dubitaverit, aut infidelitatis me arguere voluerit, paratus semper ero fidem meam palàm commonstrare, quam etiam depredeprehendent omnes, qui conferendi laborem sumere volent. Nolui omnia describere, quæ in istis scriptis passim occurrunt à receptâ doctrinâ, uti videtur, discrepantia, ne moles libelli nimium excresceret, sed ista tantùm annotavi, quæ mentem ipsorum clarissimè explicare, & ad articulorum discrepantium probationem sufficere videbantur. Subjunxi ista, suis quæque locis, Confessionis nostræ singulis Articulis, ut sententiarum collatio melius instituì, & discrepantia clariùs perspici queat, atque eum in finem numeris etiam annotavi, quibus in locis discrepantia inveniri videatur. Confessionem autem cum vetustissimis, tum Gallicis, tum Belgicis editionibus contuli, & si quæ in posterioribus omissa reperiebantur, quæ in prioribus extabant ea uncinulis, discretionis causâ inclusa, passim addidi in gratiam eorum, quibus otium non est editiones illas diversas conferre. Produxi hic Doctores, non qui in Ecclesijs Germanicis, Gallicis, Britannicis, Helveticis, alijve docent, aut aliquando docuerunt (hæc enim cura ad nos proprie non pertinet) sed qui in Ecclesijs[?] Reformatis fœderati nostri Belgij hodie docent, aut proximè elapso hoc decennio docuerunt, & qui proinde Doctrinæ suæ coram Synodo Nationali Belgicâ rationem reddere tenentur. Præcipuorum nomina in gratiam tuam, benigne Lector, hic subjicio. D. IACOBUS ARMINIUS, SS. Theologiæ Professor in Academiâ Leydensi, cujus scripta ediderunt & defenderunt Remonstrantes Leydenses. D. CONRADUS VORSTIUS, SS. Theologiæ Professor Academiæ Leydensis. M. SIMON EPISCOPIUS, SS. Theologiæ Professor in Academiâ Leydensi. M. PETRUS BERTIUS, Regens Collegij Theologici in Academiâ Leydensi. CASPARUS BARLÆUS, Subregens Collegii Theologici in Academiâ Leydensi. ADRIANUS BORRIUS, Pastor Ecclesiæ Leydensis. IOANNES ARNOLDUS, Pastor Ecclesiæ Leydensis. BERNARDUS DUINGLIO, Pastor Ecclesiæ Leydensis. IOANNES WTENBOGARDUS, Pastor Ecclesiæ Haganæ. NICOLAUS GREVINCHOVIUS, Pastor Ecclesiæ Roterodamensis. ADOLPHUS VENATOR, Pastor Ecclesiæ Alcmarianæ.
units.tr: Concerning the controversies that were stirred up among the Reformed Churches of the Belgic Churches a few years ago, and that have grievously troubled those same Churches until now, various rumours are spread abroad, not only among foreigners but also at home. The authors of these unhappy controversies, so that they may escape the odium of a deed so ill-timed and harmful, are now wholly intent on minimising them by every means, and on persuading everyone that the quarrel has been raised by them only over certain subtleties concerning that difficult doctrine of divine predestination, which are by no means necessary for promoting the salvation of men. They publicly protest that, apart from those five well-known articles on predestination and the chapters annexed to them, they have nothing about which to contend. Because these controversies have not been settled long since, they lay all the blame on those who oppose them, since, as they pretend, those who dissent will not tolerate them in articles that are less necessary to salvation. Others think they have very weighty reasons, by which they are led not merely to suspect but altogether to judge that this plausible controversy about predestination, expressed in those five articles, is only a pretext (πρόφασις), under cover of which they try to introduce Socinianism (perhaps somewhat disguised or coated over) into these Reformed Churches. They believe this all the more because, from the writings of those who signed that protestation with their own hands, they can clearly show that on far more articles these men depart from the received doctrine of these Churches and approach the errors of the Socinians; and that, not by any means so far, could they be moved to make an open and plain public declaration of what they think about the principal heads of Reformed doctrine, or how far they stand from the errors of the Socinians; and finally that they themselves profess that these arts are employed to advance their cause, so that they do not proceed further among the common people than the articles commonly known: that, according to the diversity of minds, they nourish some with milk for a long time, offer more solid food to others sooner, approach some directly and openly, and others by underground passages; with some they deal plainly and conceal nothing, or, as they say, in a round phrase; but among others they draw the accepted formulas of speech into a good sense by a convenient interpretation, so that they may learn the truth even unknowingly, and not be repelled from the very threshold by the appearance of novelty. So much so that today there is dispute over these controversies, both over their state and over their truth. What is to be made of this, God willing, the National Synod of the Belgic Churches, convened by the Illustrious and Most Powerful STATES GENERAL to examine and remove these controversies, will shortly consider and judge. I judged that I would be doing this a matter neither unwelcome nor useless if I publicly communicated those things which I had at some time noted for my private use from the public writings of the teachers of our Churches, in which they seemed to depart from the doctrine received and expressed in the Confession of our Churches. I have copied everything in good faith, as an honest man should; if anyone perhaps doubts this, or wishes to charge me with unfaithfulness, I shall always be ready to show my good faith openly, and all who are willing to take the trouble of comparing will also discover it. I have not wished to copy out everything that in these writings everywhere appears to differ from the received doctrine, lest the bulk of the book grow too large, but have noted only those passages which seemed to explain their mind most clearly and to be sufficient for proving the discrepant articles. I have added these, each in its place beside the single articles of our Confession, so that the comparison of opinions may be better made and the discrepancy may be seen more clearly; and to this end I have also marked with numbers the places where the discrepancy seems to be found. I have compared the Confession with the most ancient editions, both French and Dutch, and where anything found in the later editions had been omitted that stood in the earlier ones, I have added it throughout, enclosed in little hooks for the sake of distinction, for the benefit of those who have no leisure to compare those different editions. Here I have brought forward teachers not of the German, French, British, Helvetic or other Churches, who teach or have taught (for that care does not properly belong to us), but those who today teach in the Reformed Churches of our allied Netherlands, or taught during the decade just past, and who are therefore bound to give an account of their doctrine before the National Synod of the Belgic Churches. For your benefit, kind reader, I set down the names of the chief of them here: Dr JACOBUS ARMINIUS, Professor of Sacred Theology in the Academy of Leiden, whose writings were published and defended by the Remonstrants of Leiden. Dr CONRADUS VORSTIUS, Professor of Sacred Theology in the Academy of Leiden. Mr SIMON EPISCOPIUS, Professor of Sacred Theology in the Academy of Leiden. Mr PETRUS BERTIUS, Regent of the Theological College in the Academy of Leiden. CASPARUS BARLÆUS, Sub-regent of the Theological College in the Academy of Leiden. ADRIANUS BORRIUS, minister of the Church of Leiden. IOANNES ARNOLDUS, minister of the Church of Leiden. BERNARDUS DUINGLIO, minister of the Church of Leiden. IOANNES WTENBOGARDUS, minister of the Church of The Hague. NICOLAUS GREVINCHOVIUS, minister of the Church of Rotterdam. ADOLPHUS VENATOR, minister of the Church of Alkmaar.

units.la: AD LECTOREM.
units.tr: TO THE READER.

units.la: HENRICUS SLATIUS, Pastor Ecclesiæ Bleyswicensis.
units.tr: HENRICUS SLATIUS, Minister of the Church of Bleyswijk.

units.la: PETRUS CUPUS, Pastor Ecclesiæ Woer-danæ.
units.tr: PETRUS CUPUS, Minister of the Church of Woerden.

units.la: HENRICUS WELSINGIUS, Pastor Ec-clesiæ S. Martensdyckanæ, in diœcesi Ultrajectinâ, qui edidit Libellum FAUSTI SOCINI, de Officio hominis Christiani in hodiernis istis de Religione controversijs: cui etiam præfixit Præfationem suam, quâ Libellum hunc Evangelicis commendat, ut satis nervosè tractantem id quod auctor sibi propositerat, monetque eos ut diligenter hunc Libellum legant, & unicè attendant, non quis, sed quid dicat: docetque Evangelicos magno cum fructu hunc Libellum legere posse, utpote qui ex eo agnituri sint, multa sibi deesse adhuc ad veram Religionis puritatem: multa etiam quæ pugnent cum illâ imprudenter adhuc in cœtibus suis retineri.
units.tr: HENRICUS WELSINGIUS, Minister of the Church of St. Martensdijk, in the diocese of Utrecht, who published a little book by FAUSTUS SOCINUS, On the Duty of a Christian Man in the present controversies about religion, and prefixed to it his own preface, in which he commends the book to the Evangelicals as treating its subject with considerable vigour in the way the author intended. He urges them to read this little book carefully and to attend only to what it says, not to who says it; and he teaches that the Evangelicals can read it with great profit, since they will recognise from it that much is still lacking to the true purity of religion, and that much is found there which conflicts with what they have imprudently retained in their congregations.

units.la: VALE, candidè Lector, & sincerè judica.
units.tr: Farewell, candid reader, and judge sincerely.

units.la: CONFESSIO verè Christiana Ecclesiarum Re-formatarum BELGICÆ, Continens summam doctrinæ de DEO, & de æternâ animarum salute.
units.tr: THE CONFESSION truly Christian of the Reformed Churches of the NETHERLANDS, containing the sum of doctrine concerning God and the eternal salvation of souls.

units.la: ARTICULUS I. De Naturâ Dei.
units.tr: ARTICLE I. On the Nature of God.

units.la: CORDE credidimus, & ore confitemur, unicam, 1. esse & simplicem, 2. Essentiam spiritualem, 3. quam DEUM vocamus, æternum, incomprehensibilem, invisibilem, 4. immutabilem, 5. infinitum, 6. qui perfectissimè est sapiens, 7. justus, & bonus, ac fons omnium bonorum uberrimus.
units.tr: We believe in our heart and confess with our mouth that there is one, 1. simple, 2. spiritual essence, 3. which we call God, eternal, incomprehensible, invisible, 4. unchangeable, 5. infinite, 6. most perfectly wise, 7. just and good, and the most abundant fountain of all good things.

units.la: Contra hunc Articulum doceri videtur.
units.tr: The following is seen to be taught against this article.

units.la: 1. Non esse unicam essentiam divinam, sed esse tres essentias divinas.
units.tr: 1. That the divine essence is not one, but that there are three divine essences.

units.la: A VORSTIO, Disp.de DEO, pag. 208. Sunt tres saltem, si non plures diversæ res in DEO. Et contradictio quædam videtur esse rem ullam verè existere, quæ non habeat suam quandam propriam essentiam. AVORSTIO, Disp. de DEO pag. 38. Pater peculiarem quandam entitatem, seu quasi limitatam & restrictam essentiam habere putandus est. Idem de Filio DEI & Spiritu S. similiter existimandum est.
units.tr: From Vorstius, Disp. on God, p. 208: There are at least three, if not more, distinct things in God. And it seems a kind of contradiction for anything to truly exist that does not have its own proper essence. Vorstius, Disp. on God, p. 38: The Father must be thought to have a peculiar entity, or as it were a limited and restricted essence. The same is to be thought similarly of the Son of God and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: II. Essentiam DEI non esse simplicem, sed compositam ex subjecto & accidentibus.
units.tr: II. That the essence of God is not simple, but composed of subject and accidents.

units.la: AVORSTIO, Disp. de DEO pag. 208. Hinc porrò alia efflorescit ratio, qua docetur, Accidentia etiam quædam in DEO locum habere. Ibidem. Totidem in DEO accidentia sunt, quot decreta de rebus foris efficiendis.
units.tr: Vorstius, Disp. on God, p. 208. From this there springs another line of reasoning, by which it is taught that certain accidents also have a place in God. Ibid. There are as many accidents in God as there are decrees concerning things to be brought about outside him.

units.la: Ibidem.pag.209. Accedunt varia Scripturæ testimonia, quibus asseritur aliud & aliud in DEO esse, videlicet subjectum & accidens. Ibidem. Aliud est ipsum vivum subjectum, aliud vita ipsa in DEO. Non sunt igitur axiomata illa, vulgò pridem recepta, simpliciter & omni modo vera: In DEVM non cadere ullam diversitatem, aut compositionem: Item, Nullum in DEO accidens esse: sed quidquid in ipso est, DEVM ipsum esse.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 209. There are added various testimonies of Scripture by which it is asserted that one thing and another is in God, namely subject and accident. Ibid. One thing is the living subject itself, another is life itself in God. Therefore those axioms, long commonly received, are not simply and in every way true: that no diversity or composition falls into God; likewise, that there is no accident in God, but whatever is in him is God himself.

units.la: Ibidem.pag.ioo. Nihil vetat generatim asserere aliud atque aliud in DEO sive in DEI essentiâ esse, idque per naturæ ne-cessitatem ab æterno. Nihil etiam vetat hactenus in DEO compositionem aliquam statuere.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 100. Nothing forbids us to assert in general that one thing and another is in God or in the essence of God, and that by the necessity of nature from eternity. Nothing also forbids us hitherto to posit some composition in God.

units.la: Ibidem.pag.247. Videtur aliquid in DEO diversitatis inesse, ut aliud sit ipsa DEI substantia vivens; aliud vita seu vis illa, per quam vivit.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 247. There seems to be something of diversity in God, so that one thing is the very living substance of God, and another is the life or power by which he lives.

units.la: III. Essentiam divinam non esse merè spiritualem, sed etiam corpoream.
units.tr: III. That the divine essence is not purely spiritual, but also corporeal.

units.la: AVORSTIO, Disp. de DEO, pag. 201. Si vocabulum Corporis in significatione latiore sumamus, nihil vetat DEO etiam Corpus adscribere.
units.tr: Vorstius, Disp. on God, p. 201. If we take the word body in a broader sense, nothing forbids us to ascribe even a body to God.

units.la: Item. pag. 251. Ipse (DEVS) ex sententia Tertulliani suum corpus, id est, suam veram & solidam substantiam habet: eoq; robustum brachium & potens dextera ei sæpenumero tribuitur.
units.tr: Also, p. 251. He (God), according to the opinion of Tertullian, has his own body, that is, his own true and solid substance; and therefore a strong arm and a mighty right hand are very often attributed to him.

units.la: IV. DEVM non esse invisibilem, sed externa oculorum glorificatorum inspectione videri posse.
units.tr: IV. That God is not invisible, but can be seen by the external inspection of glorified eyes.

units.la: A VORSTIO, Disp. de DEO, pag.237. Quod ea loca, quibus DEVM visuri dicimur, de interiore mentis speculatione, non de externa oculorum inspectione vulgò interpretantur, nescio an S.literis satis consentaneum sit.
units.tr: Vorstius, Disp. on God, p. 237. That those passages in which we are said to see God are commonly interpreted of the inner contemplation of the mind, not of the external inspection of the eyes, I do not know whether is sufficiently consonant with Scripture.

units.la: Ibidem.pag.200. Quod dicitur nos DEI faciem visuros 1.Ioh.3.2. Apocal. 22.4. id quoad nos de futuro seculo intelligendum est, cum jam non amplius caro & sanguis erimus, sed ἰσάγγελοι & spirituales. Quamquam alij de visione mentis tantum, non de externa & vera contemplatione haec loca intelligunt.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 200. That it is said we shall see the face of God, 1 John 3:2; Rev. 22:4, is to be understood of us in the future age, when we shall no longer be flesh and blood, but isangelic [ἰσάγγελοι] and spiritual. Although others understand these places only of the vision of the mind, not of external and true contemplation.

units.la: Ibidem.pag.251. Si quis objiciat, At non habet DEVS formae pulchritudinem, quia invisibilis. Resp. Imò summa est ejus pulchritudo, sed quae non potest nisi à beatis Angelis & ἰσαγγέλοις hominibus videri. Et non sine causa Moses faciem eius videre cupivit.Exod.33. Et non minima felicitatis nostrae pars in visione DEI statuitur 1.Ioh.3.2.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 251. If someone objects, "But God does not have the beauty of form, because he is invisible," the answer is: on the contrary, his beauty is supreme, but it can be seen only by the blessed angels and isangelic [ἰσαγγέλοις] men. And not without reason Moses desired to see his face, Exod. 33. And no small part of our happiness is placed in the vision of God, 1 John 3:2.

units.la: Apolog.Exeg.cap.6.pag.26. 27. Nec eos facile damnandos esse crediderim, qui loca superius citata (Apocal.22. Matth. 5. & 18.1. Ioh.3. Psalm.16. & 17.) & alia eodem pertinentia, non de interna tantum mentis speculatione, sed potissimum de externa oculorum inspectione, seu verâ faciei contemplatione simpliciter accipere solent. Non mortalibus, quamdiu tales sunt, & in hoc seculo degunt, haec visio unquam tribuenda est (quippe qui carnalibus oculis hisce ad lucem illam inaccessam penetrare, DEVMque videre non possunt 1.Tim.6.) sed solis immortalibus ac beatis, hoc est, ijs tantùm, quorum oculi & tota corpora spiritualia fore dicuntur.1.Corinth.15.
units.tr: Apology, Exeg. ch. 6, pp. 26, 27. Nor would I readily believe that those should be condemned who are accustomed to take simply the places cited above (Rev. 22; Matt. 5 and 18; 1 John 3; Psalms 16 and 17) and others pertaining to the same, not only of the inner speculation of the mind, but chiefly of the external inspection of the eyes, or the true contemplation of the face. This vision is never to be ascribed to mortals, as long as they are such and dwell in this age (for they cannot penetrate with these carnal eyes to that inaccessible light and see God, 1 Tim. 6), but only to the immortal and blessed, that is, to those alone whose eyes and whole bodies are said to be spiritual, 1 Cor. 15.

units.la: V. DEVM non esse immutabilem.
units.tr: V. That God is not unchangeable.

units.la: A VORSTIO, Disp.de DEO, pag.212. Quinta species mutationis (alteratio) eatenus in DEO locum habere potest, quatenus ipse actiones quasdam immanentes exercet juxta liberam voluntatem.
units.tr: Vorstius, Disp. on God, p. 212. The fifth kind of change (alteration) can have a place in God so far as he exercises certain immanent actions according to his free will.

units.la: Ibidem. Haec voluntas DEI semper principium cujusdam mutabilitatis est etiam in ipso DEO.
units.tr: Ibid. This will of God is always the principle of a certain mutability even in God himself.

units.la: Ibidem. Non satis igitur circumspecte loquuntur, qui DEUM, ut essentia, sic etiam voluntate, prorsus immutabilem esse affirmant.
units.tr: Ibid. Therefore those speak not sufficiently cautiously who affirm that God, as in essence, so also in will, is absolutely unchangeable.

units.la: Ibidem. pag. 213. Haec voluntas DEI in DEO non minus quam in Angelis & hominibus ad opposita vertibilis est.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 213. This will of God in God is no less capable of being turned to opposites than in angels and men.

units.la: Ibidem. Absoluta & simplex immutabilitas hac in parte DEO attribui non potest.
units.tr: Ibid. Absolute and simple immutability cannot be attributed to God in this respect.

units.la: Ibidem. Respondeo, hinc (ex infinitate DEI) non pro-bari omnimodam & absolutam essentiae immutabilitatem.
units.tr: Ibid. I reply: hence (from the infinity of God) it is not proved that there is an absolute and entire immutability of essence.

units.la: Ibidem. pag. 306. Quae sub conditione DEUS vult fa-cere, vel quae fieri tantum desiderat, vel quae etiam fortasse indefinita relinquit, in iis aliquo modo mutabilis est DEI voluntas.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 306. Those things which God wills to do under a condition, or which he merely desires to be done, or which perhaps he leaves undetermined, in these the will of God is in some way mutable.

units.la: Ibidem. pag. 312. Nihil absurdi ex eo sequitur, quod DEUS in tempore quaedam praecise ac definitè velle vel nolle dicitur, quae fortassis antea non ita praecisè vel voluit vel noluit: quemadmodum nec absurdum est DEUM nunc quaedam in specie velle desinere, quae antea reipsa voluit.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 312. Nothing absurd follows from this, that God is said in time to will or not will certain things precisely and definitely, which perhaps before he did not will or not will so precisely; just as it is not absurd that God now ceases to will certain particular things which he really willed before.

units.la: Ibidem. pag. 451. Moses ipsum DEUM à proposito perden-di populi inter alia revocasse dicitur, argumento metuendi mali eventus: quod scilicet hostes DEUM essent calumniaturi, &c. Videtur enim DEUS hunc eventum ut-pote sua natura possibilem suo modo metuisse & propterea à proposito suo recessisse.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 451. Moses is said to have turned God back from his purpose of destroying the people, among other reasons, on the ground of fear of an evil outcome: namely, that the enemies would slander God, etc. For God seems to have feared this outcome, as being possible in its own nature, in its own way, and therefore to have withdrawn from his purpose.

units.la: Ibidem. DEUS suo modo aliquando metuit, hoc est, me-rito suspicatur, & prudenter conjicit, hoc vel illud malum oriturum, ex aliquo suo opere, si ipsum forte procedat; eoq; opus ipsum jam inceptum deserit aut immutat.
units.tr: Ibid. God in his own way sometimes fears, that is, rightly suspects and prudently conjectures that this or that evil will arise from some work of his, if it perhaps proceeds; and therefore he abandons or changes the work itself already begun.

units.la: Ab ARMINIO, contra Perk. pag. 195. DEUS vult serio, ut omnes homines salventur, at compulsus pertinaci & in-corrigibili malitia nonnullorum vult illos jacturam facere salutis, hoc est, condemnari.
units.tr: From Arminius, against Perkins, p. 195. God seriously wills that all men be saved, but, compelled by the stubborn and incorrigible malice of some, he wills that they suffer loss of salvation, that is, be condemned.

units.la: Ab Episcopio, Disp. de Volunt. Dei, Thes. 7. Voluntes aliquae Dei certo quodam tempore desinunt.
units.tr: From Episcopius, Disp. on the Will of God, Thesis 7. Some wills of God cease at a certain time.

units.la: Ibidem. Thes. 21, Ineptum & ridiculum est dicere seriam & Veram voluntatem Dei esse nequire, nisi effectum sortiatur.
units.tr: Ibid., Thesis 21. It is foolish and ridiculous to say that the serious and true will of God cannot be, unless it obtains its effect.

units.la: IV. Dei essentiam non esse infinitam seu immensam, neque ubique, sed tantum in coelo, praesentem.
units.tr: IV. That the essence of God is not infinite or immense, nor everywhere, but present only in heaven.

units.la: A Vorstio, Disp. de Deo, pag. 214. Non caret controversia id, quod hic assumitur pro certo, videlicet, Essentiam Dei prorsus & simpliciter immensam esse.
units.tr: From Vorstius, Disp. de Deo, p. 214. What is here assumed as certain is not free from controversy, namely, that the essence of God is wholly and simply immense.

units.la: Ibidem pag. 132. Excipi potest (ad loca Scripturae, quae agunt de Omnipraesentia Dei) nusquam diserte in Scriptura doceri Deum substantialiter ubiq; praesentem, adeoque simpliciter infinitum esse. Nusquam scriptum legimus, Dei substantiam simpliciter immensam, & totam reipsa omnibus in locis praesentem esse, imo non pauca, quae contrarium sensum habere videntur, passim occurrunt.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 132. It may be objected (with regard to the passages of Scripture that treat of the omnipresence of God) that nowhere in Scripture is it plainly taught that God is substantially present everywhere, and therefore simply infinite. Nowhere do we read that the substance of God is simply immense and in reality wholly present in all places. Indeed, not a few passages that seem to have the contrary sense occur everywhere.

units.la: Ibidem. pag. 133. Dei Majestas ideo templis manufactis includi non potest, quia substantialiter in altissimo illo coelo, tanquam in solio aut palatio suo resideat: sic tamen ut virtualiter etiam sive κατ᾽ ἐνέργειαν [?] suam in terra versetur.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 133. The majesty of God cannot be contained in temples made by hands, because he resides substantially in that highest heaven, as in his throne or palace; yet in such a way that he also dwells virtually, or by his energy [κατ᾽ ἐνέργειαν] [?], on earth.

units.la: Ibidem. Patet ex Scripturis immensitatem aut ubiquitatem essentiae divinae probari non posse.
units.tr: Ibid. It is clear that the immensity or ubiquity of the divine essence cannot be proved from Scripture.

units.la: Ibidem pag. 234. Essentiae divinae immensitas inter ea quae simpliciter ἀδύνατα dicuntur, merito referitur.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 234. The immensity of the divine essence is rightly reckoned among those things that are called absolutely impossible [ἀδύνατα].

units.la: Ibidem. Deus non est actu simpliciter infinitus, neque essendo, neque operando.
units.tr: Ibid. God is not actually simply infinite, neither in his being nor in his working.

units.la: Ibidem pag. 235. Deus est quidem infinitus diuturnitate; quia sic ordo & natura postulat: sed non propterea est immensa essentia, quia hoc natura potius aversatur.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 235. God is indeed infinite in duration, since order and nature require it; but he is not on that account an immense essence, because nature rather shrinks from this.

units.la: Ibidem. Non sequitur Deum immediate illic sua substantia adesse, ubicunque operatur: quia per causas medias, sive physicas, sive hyperphysicas, puta Angelos &c. operari potest, ut Rex aliquis per suos ministros.
units.tr: Ibid. It does not follow that God is immediately present there in his substance wherever he works, since he can work through middle causes, whether physical or hyperphysical, namely angels and the like, as some king works through his ministers.

units.la: Ibidem. Apparet saltem incertum & dubium esse quod vulgò de substantiali DEI immensitate traditur.
units.tr: Ibid. It appears at least uncertain and doubtful what is commonly taught about the substantial immensity of God.

units.la: Ibidem. Prima probatio nititur ijs Scripturæ locis, quibus affirmari omninò videtur DEUM ratione substantiæ suæ TANTUM in cœlo esse, sive in cœlesti Paradiso.
units.tr: Ibid. The first proof rests on those passages of Scripture by which it seems wholly affirmed that God, in respect of his substance, is ONLY in heaven, or in the heavenly Paradise.

units.la: Ibidem.pag.237. Simpliciter credamus, quod S. literæ totiès inculcant, DEUM revera suâ substantiâ (quæ ut am-plissima & maxima, nostrique respectu immensa est) in cœlo altissimo, eodemque capacissimo habitare: in terrâ verò ubique virtute & sapientiâ suâ, sive efficaci operatione & providentiâ suâ nobis adesse.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 237. Let us simply believe what the Holy Scriptures so often insist on: that God truly dwells in his substance (which, as most ample and greatest, and immense in relation to us) in the highest heaven, which is most capacious; but on earth he is present to us everywhere by his power and wisdom, that is, by his effective operation and providence.

units.la: Ibidem.pag.238. Sacræ litteræ DEUM quidem magnum, excelsum, elevatum vocant, sed nunquam absolutè infini-tum, aut simpliciter immensum appellant. Nam secundum quid, & comparativè dici posse infinitum non negamus, sicut respectu nostri infinitus est numerus stellarum, & arenæ maris.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 238. Holy Scripture indeed calls God great, high and exalted, but never calls him absolutely infinite or simply immense. For we do not deny that he can be called infinite in a certain respect and comparatively, just as with respect to us the number of the stars and the sand of the sea is infinite.

units.la: Ibidem.pag.239. Sanè de loco & localiprasentiâ, quin DEO verè & rectè attribui possit, minimè dubitandum videtur.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 239. Surely there seems to be no doubt that place and local presence can truly and rightly be attributed to God.

units.la: Antapo. 1. pag. 127. Ad locum in genere acceptum ipse DEUS aptissimè referri potest.
units.tr: Antapol. 1, p. 127. God himself can very aptly be referred to place taken in general.

units.la: Disp. de DEO, pag. 240. Quid vetat spiritualem quoque DEI essentiam habere suam propriam quantitatem. Ibidem. pag.241. Cum DEUS, etiam quâ DEUS, hoc est, respe-ctu substantiæ suæ magnus esse dicitur, certè aliquam hîc quantitatem & cogitari & esse oportet.
units.tr: Disp. de Deo, p. 240. What prevents the spiritual essence of God from having its own proper quantity? Ibid., p. 241. Since God, even as God, that is, in respect of his substance, is said to be great, certainly some quantity must both be conceived and exist here.

units.la: Ab EPISCOPIO, Disp. priv. de DEO Thes. 10. Non credimus absolutè scitu necessaria esse, quæ de immensitatis divinæ modis, & de omnipræsentiâ essentiâ controvertun-tur.
units.tr: From Episcopius, Disp. priv. de Deo, Thes. 10. We do not believe that those things are absolutely necessary to know which are disputed concerning the modes of divine immensity and the omnipresence of the essence.

units.la: A SLATIO, Epist. ad N. 9. Mart. & 30. Iun. 1608. Constat DEI manum & potentiam ubique esse, siquidem Spiritu oris sui ubique est: non secus ac Sol ubivis locorum in terris est, non secundum essentiam suam, sed secundum virtutem suam & potentiam. Ut verum dicam, non est cur sententiam illam improbem. Video namque perfectio-nem rerum mundanarum in hoc esse, ut potentia sua ulte-rius quam essentia extendantur; quam perfectionem proculdubio à DEO habent, qui istas ad imaginem suam cre-avit. Et quo majores sunt potentiae, seque latius exten-dunt, eò perfectiores & imagini suae magis conformes sunt: veluti suaveolentes atque medicinales herbae, la-pides, flores, &c. Atqui ego quidem existimo DEUM tunc perfectiorem fieri, quando dicitur operari posse, videre, audire, ubi sua essentia non est, quàm cum dicitur es-sentia sua praesentiam requiri ad operandum, videndum, aut audiendum.
units.tr: From Slatius, Letter to N., 9 March and 30 June 1608. It is agreed that the hand and power of God is everywhere, since by the Spirit of his mouth he is everywhere: just as the sun is everywhere on earth, not according to its essence, but according to its virtue and power. To speak the truth, there is no reason why I should condemn that opinion. For I see that the perfection of worldly things lies in this, that their power extends further than their essence; which perfection they undoubtedly have from God, who created them in his image. And the greater the powers and the more widely they extend, the more perfect they are and the more conformed to his image: as fragrant and medicinal herbs, stones, flowers, etc. But I indeed think that God becomes more perfect when it is said that he can work, see and hear where his essence is not, than when it is said that his essence is required for working, seeing or hearing.

units.la: VII. DEUM non omnia & singula certò praescire, sed quaedam verè sperare, expectare, metuere, & suspicari; & quaedam scire per discursum: ac proinde non esse perfectis-simè sapientem.
units.tr: VII. That God does not foreknow all and each thing with certainty, but truly hopes, expects, fears and suspects some things, and knows some things by discursive reasoning; and therefore is not most perfectly wise.

units.la: AVORSTIO, Disp. de DEO, pag.311. Sapientia DEI per se minimè requirit, ut DEUS omnia & singula, quaecunque nunc in mundo fiunt, ab aeterno scientiâ visionis ab-solutâ praenoverit.
units.tr: From Vorstius, Disp. de Deo, p. 311. The wisdom of God does not by itself at all require that God from eternity foreknew, by absolute knowledge of vision, all and each of the things that now happen in the world.

units.la: Ibidem. Nihil vetat etiam in DEO (generatim loquen-do) aliquem talem esse discursum, quo unum post aliud, & rursus unum propter aliud, aut esse aut fieri velit. Imò sana ratio exigit, ut quia vera proaeresis in DEO locum habet, respectu eorum omnium quae sunt aut fiunt extra ipsam, etiam dianoia quaedam, sed divina & ab omni defectu liberrima, locum in ipso inveniat. Ibidem.pag.271. Videtur omninò quaedam dianoia, sed merè divina, & nostrae valdè dissimilis esse in DEO.
units.tr: Ibid. Nothing prevents there being in God (speaking generally) some such discursive reasoning, by which he wills one thing after another, and again one on account of another, to be or to become. Indeed, sound reason demands that, since a true deliberation (proairesis) has a place in God with respect to all those things which are or happen outside him, some thinking [διάνοια] also, but divine and most free from all defect, should find a place in him. Ibid., p. 271. It seems altogether that there is some thinking [διάνοια], but purely divine and very unlike ours, in God.

units.la: Ibidem. pag.441. Plenius respondere videntur, qui certam quidem in genere universam DEI scientiam esse docent, sed ita tamen ut plures certitudinis causas in visione praesentium, ac praeteritorum, quam in visione futuro-rum contingentium agnoscant, atque ita horum spem atque expectationem comparativè loquendo aliquatenus incertam esse statuunt: namque quatenus ipsa opera, quæ futu-ra sperantur, nondum reipsa existunt: imò quatenus re-spectu suarum causarum, à quibus proximè sive imme-diatè pendent, merè contingentia sunt, hoc est, tam non fieri, quam fieri possunt: nec per absolutum aliquod decretum ad alterutram partem præcisè determinata sunt. Quo sanè respectu vera & proprie dicta spes sive expe-ctatio DEO attribui potest.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 441. They seem to answer more fully who teach that God's knowledge in general is certainly universal, but acknowledge that there are more causes of certainty in the vision of present and past things than in the vision of future contingent things, and so declare that their hope and expectation are, speaking comparatively, somewhat uncertain. For insofar as the works themselves that are hoped for as future do not yet actually exist; indeed, insofar as, with respect to their causes on which they depend most immediately, they are merely contingent, that is, they can both not happen and happen, nor are they precisely determined to either side by any absolute decree. In this respect certainly true and properly so-called hope or expectation can be attributed to God.

units.la: Ibidem. Quod de spe sive expectatione DEI diximus, idem suo modo de optatione seu desiderio DEI statuendum est.
units.tr: Ibid. What we have said of hope or expectation in God, the same must be established in its own way concerning the desire or wish of God.

units.la: Ibidem pag. 451. DEUS suo modo aliquando metuit, hoc est, merito suspicatur & prudenter conjicit, hoc vel illud malum oriturum. Ibidem. Quatenus & quo sensu Spes in DEUM cadit, eatenus & eodem sensu metus seu ti-mor eidem attribui potest.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 451. God in his own way sometimes fears, that is, rightly suspects and prudently conjectures that this or that evil will arise. Ibid. Insofar as, and in what sense, hope falls upon God, in that measure and in the same sense fear or dread can be attributed to him.

units.la: Ibidem pag. 266. Absit ut DEO vel hypocrisin, vel te-meritatem, atque imprudentiam ejusmodi attribuamus, cujusmodi per infallibilem omnium futurorum prænotionem induci omninò videtur.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 266. Far be it from us to attribute to God either hypocrisy or such rashness and imprudence as seems altogether to be induced by infallible foreknowledge of all future things.

units.la: Ibidem pag. 275. Qui præscientiam DEI universaliter si-mul & æqualiter, sive prorsus eodem modo ad omnia quæcunque siunt, tam necessaria quam contingentia, tam mala quam bona, sine delectu extendunt, illi arbitrij no-stri libertatem, omnemque rerum contingentiam ever-tunt; imò DEUM ipsum peccati auctorem tandem ma-nifestè constituunt.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 275. Those who extend the foreknowledge of God universally, at the same time and equally, or altogether in the same way, to all things whatsoever that happen, both necessary and contingent, both evil and good, without distinction, overthrow the liberty of our will and all contingency of things; indeed, in the end they plainly make God himself the author of sin.

units.la: Neque vero respectus decreti & præscientia divina quidquam facere nobis videntur, ad hoc, ut actus liberi, necessarij etiam dici possint.
units.tr: Nor indeed do the respect of the decree and divine foreknowledge seem to us to make anything such that free acts could also be called necessary.

units.la: Disput. privat. de DEO, Thef. 10. Inter quæ (scitu non necessaria) an referri non debeat operosa illa quæstio de scientia futurorum contingentium absoluta & conditionata disquiri permittimus.
units.tr: Disput. privat. de Deo, Thes. 10. Among those matters (not necessary to know) we allow that the laborious question about the knowledge of future contingent things, whether absolute or conditional, may be inquired into.

units.la: ARTICULUS II. De Cognitione DEI.
units.tr: ARTICLE II. On the Knowledge of God.

units.la: Duobus autem modis DEVM cognoscimus: primò per ipsam creationem, conservationem, & gubernationem universi huius mundi. Is enim oculis nostris est instar Libri pulcherrimi, in quo creaturæ omnes, à minimis usq; ad maximas, veluti literæ quædam sunt inscriptæ, ex quibus invisibilia DEI conspici & cognosci possunt; nempè æterna ipsius potentia & divinitas, ut Apostolus Paulus loquitur, Rom. 1.20.1. Quæ omnia sufficiunt ad homines convincendos & inexcusabiles reddendos. Secundò seipsum multò clarius & manifestius in sacro suo & divino verbo nobis cognoscendum præbet ac patefacit, quantum scilicet nobis in hac vitâ ad ipsius gloriam & ad suorum salutem necessarium est.
units.tr: We know God in two ways. First, through the creation, preservation and government of this whole world. For it is to our eyes like a most beautiful book, in which all creatures, from the smallest to the greatest, are written as letters, from which the invisible things of God can be seen and known: namely his eternal power and divinity, as the Apostle Paul says, Rom. 1.20. These things are enough to convict men and render them inexcusable. Second, in his holy and divine Word he presents and reveals himself to us to be known much more clearly and manifestly, namely as much as is necessary for us in this life for his glory and for the salvation of his people.

units.la: Contra hunc Articulum doceri videtur.
units.tr: The following seems to be taught against this Article.

units.la: 1. Nullam omninò haberi posse notitiam de DEO, sine supernaturali revelatione.
units.tr: 1. That no knowledge of God whatever can be had without supernatural revelation.

units.la: A VORSTIO, Disp. de DEO, pag. 128. Non existimamus innatam esse nobis aliquam Dei notitiam.Ibidem. Etiam-num integræ nationes inveniuntur, quæ nullam Divinitatis opinionem habere videntur.
units.tr: From VORSTIUS, Disp. de Deo, p. 128. We do not think that any knowledge of God is innate in us. Ibidem. Even now there are whole nations which seem to have no notion of the Godhead at all.

units.la: Apolog. Exeg. pag.5. Semper patefactio aliqua tum naturalis, tum supernaturalis, ipsam Dei notitiam præcedit necessario.
units.tr: Apolog. Exeg. p. 5. Always some revelation, both natural and supernatural, necessarily precedes the knowledge of God itself.

units.la: Paraphr.ad Rom.1.20. Tametsi enim præcipuæ Dei virtutes, puta æterna ipsius potentia, & divina ejusdem voluntas inde à creatione mundi aliquo modo occultæ ac velut invisibiles fuerunt, nunc tamen hæ virtutes ex iis, quæ per Christum & Apostolos facta fuerunt, clarè intel-lectæ perspiciuntur. Unde fit ut impij & injusti illi nullam impietatis suæ excusationem in medium afferre pos-sint.
units.tr: Paraphrase on Rom. 1.20. For although the chief virtues of God, namely his eternal power and his divine will, were in some way hidden from the creation of the world and as it were invisible, yet now these virtues are clearly understood and perceived from those things which were done through Christ and the Apostles. Hence those impious and unjust men have no excuse for their impiety that they can bring forward.

units.la: Schol. ad Rom.1.20. τὰ γὰρ ἀόρατα.] Hæc verba prole-psin continent, quâ Apostolus concedit hactenus quodammodo invisibilia & occulta fuisse, quæ nunc in Evangelio clarè revelata sunt. Itaque comma ponendum est post nomen Κόσμος[?], & prima ista verba sic interpretanda sunt. Quæ enim ipsius invisibilia fuerunt inde à creatione mundi. Phrasin prorsus similem vide Matth.13.35.
units.tr: Scholion on Rom. 1.20, "for the invisible things" [τὰ γὰρ ἀόρατα]. These words contain a prolepsis, by which the Apostle concedes that these things were hitherto in some way invisible and hidden, but are now clearly revealed in the Gospel. Therefore a comma must be placed after the word "world" [Κόσμος], and these first words must be interpreted thus: For those things of his which were invisible from the creation of the world. See a phrase entirely similar at Matt. 13.35.

units.la: Τοῖς[?] ποιήμασι] Intelligit omnia ea, quæ tum à Christo, tum ab Apostolis facta fuerunt ad Evangelij confirmatio-nem. Confer.Act.2.22.
units.tr: "To the works" [τοῖς ποιήμασι]. He means all those things which were done both by Christ and by the Apostles to confirm the Gospel. Compare Acts 2.22.

units.la: Αἱ διὰ αὐτῆς δύναμις[?]] His duobus nominibus completitur Apostolus duas primarias Evangelij partes, nempe divina promissa & præcepta. Æterna enim potentia Dei significat illam Dei virtutem, quâ servat ab æternâ mor-te, quicunque ipsi adhærent. Confer.Ephes.1.20. Per Divinitatem autem nihil aliud quam divina voluntas, quæ solidè nobis in Christo patefacta est, significatur. Confer Col.2.9. Ephes.3.19. Hæc explicatio est Socini contra Wiek.pag.341.342. Catech.Racov.pag.23.24.
units.tr: "Eternal power" [ἀΐδιος δύναμις]. By these two terms the Apostle completes the two chief parts of the Gospel, namely divine promises and precepts. For eternal power signifies that power of God by which he preserves from eternal death all who cling to him. Compare Eph. 1.20. By divinity, however, nothing else is signified than the divine will, which has been solidly revealed to us in Christ. Compare Col. 2.9; Eph. 3.19. This explanation is that of Socinus against Wiek, pp. 341–342; Racovian Catechism, pp. 23–24.

units.la: A SIM. EPISCOPIO, Disp.priv. de cognit. DEI, corol.2. 3.An cognitio DEI sit naturalis? Distinguimus. An cognitio Dei, quæ ex naturâ habetur, sit naturalis? Ne-gamus.
units.tr: From SIMON EPISCOPIUS, Private disputation on the knowledge of God, corollary 2. 3. Is the knowledge of God natural? We distinguish. Is the knowledge of God which is had from nature natural? We deny.

units.la: ARTICVLVS III. De Sacrâ Scripturâ.
units.tr: ARTICLE III. On Holy Scripture.

units.la: CONfitemur hoc Dei verbum non fuisse ullâ humanâ voluntate aut allatum aut traditum: sed sanctos Dei viros divino afflatos Spiritu illud elocutos esse, ut testatur divus Petrus 1. Postea verò Deus ipse pro immensâ suâ curâ & sollicitudine, quam de suis, suorumque salute gerit, servis suis Prophetis & Apostolis mandavit, ut sua ille oracula scriptis committerent: ipseque adeò duas tabulas Legis, digito suo exaravit: quæ causa est cur ejusmodi scripta sacram & divinam Scripturam appellamus.
units.tr: We confess that this Word of God was never brought forth or handed down by any human will, but that holy men of God, moved by the divine Spirit, spoke it, as the divine Peter testifies, 1. Afterwards, however, God himself, out of his immense care and concern for the salvation of his own and their servants, commanded his Prophets and Apostles to commit his oracles to writing; and he himself indeed wrote the two tables of the Law with his own finger. This is why we call such writings sacred and divine Scripture.

units.la: Contra hunc Articulum doceri videtur.
units.tr: The following seems to be taught against this Article.

units.la: 1. Prophetas & Apostolos S. Scripturæ Scriptores in scribendo non semper, velubique, actos a Spiritu S. sed in nonnullis potuisse errare.
units.tr: 1. The Prophets and Apostles, the writers of Holy Scripture, were not always and everywhere moved by the Holy Spirit in writing, but could have erred in some matters.

units.la: A VORSTIO, Libello de Autor. S. Script. Steinf. ed. p. 15. Quamvis in quibusdam paucis rebus, quæ nullius sunt ponderis (quum fieri posset, ut alius alio talium rerum veritatem melius tenuerit) fortasse aliquantum aut etiam multum diversè alius ab alio scripserint. Ibidem.pag.104. Fieri posset, ut verissima ea omnia essent, quæ de ipsis historia affirmat, & tamen ipsi nonnunquam hac in parte (in interpretatione locorum aliquorum V. T. & explicatione argumentorum inde ductorum) leuiter errassent.
units.tr: From VORSTIUS, On the Authors of Holy Scripture, Steinfurt ed., p. 15. Although in a few matters of no weight (since it could happen that one held the truth of such things better than another), perhaps one wrote somewhat, or even quite differently, from another. Ibidem, p. 104. It could be that all those things were entirely true which history affirms about them, and yet they themselves sometimes erred slightly in this part (in the interpretation of some passages of the Old Testament and the explanation of arguments drawn from them).

units.la: P. CVPVS affirmavit Ioanni Taurino, esse inter REMONSTRANTES, qui dubitent de ἀὐτοπιστία[?] S. Scripturæ.
units.tr: P. CUPUS affirmed to John Taurinus that there are among the REMONSTRANTS some who doubt the self-authentication [αὐτοπιστία] of Holy Scripture.

units.la: I. ARMINIVS affirmavit, in publicâ disputatione, Apostolos quædam scripsisse non ex instinctu Spiritus sancti, quod probare conabatur ex 1. Corinth.7.12.
units.tr: I. ARMINIUS affirmed in a public disputation that the Apostles wrote some things not from the impulse of the Holy Spirit, which he tried to prove from 1 Cor. 7.12.

units.la: ARTICVLVS IV. De Canonicis Libris Vet. & Novi Testamenti.
units.tr: ARTICLE IV. On the Canonical Books of the Old and New Testament.

units.la: COmplectimur autem sacram Scriptu-ram duobus illis voluminibus Veteris & Novi Testamenti, qui libri CANONICI vocantur, de quibus nulla est controversia. Eorum hic est tum numerus, tum ordo in Ecclesia DEI receptus. Quinque libri Moysis, liber Iosuæ, Iudicum, Ruth, duo libri Samuelis, duo Regum, duo Chronicorum, qui & Paralipomenon vocantur, primus Esdræ, Nehemias, Esther, Iob: item Psalmi Davidis, tres libri Salomonis, nempe Proverbia, Ecclesia-stes, & Canticum Canticorum: quatuor Prophe-ta Majotæ Majores, Esaias, Ieremias, Ezechiel & Daniel: adhæc duodecim etiam Minores Prophetæ. Novi porrò Testamenti libri Canonici sunt, Evangelistæ quatuor, divus scilicet Matthæus, Marcus, Lucas, & Iohannes: Acta Apostolorum: quatuordecim Epistolæ divi Pauli, & septem reliquorum Apostolorum: Apocalypsis divi Iohannis Apostoli.
units.tr: We embrace, moreover, Holy Scripture in those two volumes of the Old and New Testament which are called the CANONICAL books, about which there is no controversy. Both the number and the order of these are received in the Church of God. The five books of Moses, the book of Joshua, Judges, Ruth, the two books of Samuel, the two of Kings, the two of Chronicles, which are also called Paralipomenon, the first (book) of Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Job; likewise the Psalms of David, the three books of Solomon, namely Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs; the four greater Prophets, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and Daniel; besides these also the twelve Minor Prophets. The canonical books of the New Testament are: the four Evangelists, namely St. Matthew, Mark, Luke and John; the Acts of the Apostles; the fourteen Epistles of St. Paul and seven of the remaining Apostles; the Apocalypse of St. John the Apostle.

units.la: REMONSTRANTES quidam dubitare videntur de Canonicâ autoritate nonnullorû librorum N.Testam. atque imprimis Epistolæ ad Hebræos, cujus autorem nonnemo inter ipsos dixit non videri scriptorem canonicum, quia cap. VII. ineptis utatur argumentationibus.
units.tr: Some of the REMONSTRANTS seem to doubt the canonical authority of some of the books of the New Testament, and especially of the Epistle to the Hebrews, whose author, one of them said, did not seem to be a canonical writer, because in chapter VII he uses inept arguments.

units.la: ARTICVLVS V. De Auctoritate S. Scriptura.
units.tr: Article V. On the Authority of Holy Scripture.

units.la: Hosce Libros solos recipimus tanquam sacros & Canonicos, quibus fides nostra inniti, confirmari,& stabiliri possit. Et credimus absque ullâ dubitatione ea omnia, quæ in illis continentur: idq; non tam quod Ecclesia illos pro Canonicis recipiat & comprobet, quàm quod Spiritus Sanctus nostris conscientijs testetur, illos à Deo emanasse: & eo etiam quod ipsi hanc suam autoautoritatem per se satis testentur ac compro-bent: quum & ipsi cæci rerum omnium, quæ in illis prædictæ fuerunt, impletionem & ex-ecutionem clarè conspicere, & veluti sensi-bus percipere possint.
units.tr: We receive these books alone as sacred and canonical, on which our faith may rest, be confirmed, and be established. And we believe without any doubt all those things which are contained in them: and this not so much because the Church receives and approves them as canonical, as because the Holy Spirit testifies to our consciences that they have proceeded from God; and also because they themselves sufficiently attest and prove their own authority through themselves, since even the blind can clearly behold the fulfilment and execution of all the things foretold in them, and can perceive them, as it were, with their senses.

units.la: ARTICULUS VI. De discrimine Librorum Canonicorum & Apocryphorum.
units.tr: Article VI. On the distinction between the Canonical and the Apocryphal Books.

units.la: Differentiam porrò constituimus inter libros hosce sacros, & eos quos Apocryphos vocant: utpote quod Apocryphos legere quidem Ecclesia possit, & documenta ex iis desumere in rebus, quæ consentiunt cum libris Canonicis: at nequaquam ea est ipsorum autoritas & firmitudo, ut ex illorum testimonio aliquod dogma de fide & Religione Christiana certò constitui possit: tantum abest, ut aliorum autoritatem infringere vel minuere valeant.
units.tr: Furthermore, we make a difference between these sacred books and those which they call Apocryphal: namely, that the Church may indeed read the Apocryphal books and draw teachings from them in matters that agree with the canonical books, but their authority and firmness are by no means such that any doctrine concerning the faith and the Christian religion can be firmly established from their testimony; much less are they able to weaken or diminish the authority of the others.

units.la: Nonnemo inter REMONSTRANTES dixit in quadam collatione, se non credere propterea aliquid verum esse, quod Apostolus Paulus id scribat.
units.tr: In a certain conference one of the Remonstrants said that he did not believe something to be true merely because the Apostle Paul wrote it.

units.la: ARTICULUS VII. De Perfectione S.Scripturæ.
units.tr: Article VII. On the Perfection of Holy Scripture.

units.la: CRedimus etiam sacrā hanc Scripturam perfectissimè omnem Dei voluntatem complecti, & in illâ abundè ea omnia doceri, quæcunque ab hominibus credi necesse est, ut salutem consequantur. Itaque cum illic exactissimè & fusè descripta sit omnis divini cultus ratio, quam Deus à fidelibus exigit: nulli hominum (quamvis Apostolicâ dignitate prædito, ac ne ulli quidem Angelo è cœlo dimisso; ut divus Paulus loquitur) fas est aliter docere, quam jam pridem in sacris Scripturis edocti sumus. Quum enim vetitum sit, ne quis Dei verbo quidquam aut addat, aut detrahat, satis eo ipso declaratur sacram hanc doctrinam omnibus suis numeris & partibus perfectam ac absolutam esse. [Unusquisque itaque diligenter cavere debet, ne quid illi addat aut detrahat, quo sapientia humana cum sapientiâ divinâ commisceri possit.] Ideóque cum hisce divinis Scripturis, atque hac Dei veritate nulla alia hominum, quantavis fan-ctitate præditorum, scripta, nulla consue-tudo, nec multitudo ulla, nec antiquitas, neq; temporum præscriptio, nec personarum successio, neque concilia ulla, nulla denique hominum decreta aut statuta conferenda aut comparanda sunt, utpote quod DEI veritas rebus omnibus antecellat. Omnes enim homines sunt mendaces, [& illorum sapientia DEO subjici non potest] sunt ipsâ vanitate vaniores. Idcirco toto animo rejicimus quæcunque cum certissimâ hac regulâ non conveniunt, uti ab Apostolis edocti, quum dicunt: Probate Spiritus, an ex DEO sint: Et, Si quis venit ad vos, & hanc doctrinam non adfert, ne recipite eum domum, &c.
units.tr: We also believe that this holy Scripture most perfectly embraces the whole will of God, and that in it abundantly all those things are taught which men must believe in order to obtain salvation. Therefore, since in it the whole manner of divine worship which God requires of the faithful has been described most exactly and at length, it is not lawful for any man, though endowed with apostolic dignity, nor even for any angel sent down from heaven (as the divine Paul puts it), to teach otherwise than we have long since been taught in the holy Scriptures. For since it is forbidden that anyone add anything to or take anything from the Word of God, this very fact sufficiently declares that this sacred doctrine is perfect and complete in all its parts and aspects. [Let each one therefore take diligent care not to add to it or take from it anything by which human wisdom might be mingled with divine wisdom.] Hence no other writings of men, however holy they may be, no custom, no multitude, no antiquity, no prescription of times, no succession of persons, no councils, and finally no decrees or statutes of men are to be set beside or compared with these divine Scriptures and this truth of God, since the truth of God surpasses all things. For all men are liars, [and their wisdom cannot be subjected to God]; they are more vain than vanity itself. Therefore with our whole heart we reject whatever does not agree with this most certain rule, as we have been taught by the Apostles when they say: Test the spirits, whether they are of God; and, If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not receive him into your house, etc.

units.la: ARTICULUS VIII. De SS. Trinitate Personarum in unicâ Essentiâ Divinâ.
units.tr: Article VIII. On the Holy Trinity of Persons in the One Divine Essence.

units.la: Iuxta hanc Veritatem, & Verbum hoc DEI, credimus in unicum solum DEVM, qui unica atque æterna est essentia, distincta reipsa, verè, & ab æterno in tres Personas, quarum quæque suas habet proprietates incommunicabiles, nempe in Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum Sanctum. 1. Pater caussa & origo & initium est omnium rerum tam visibilium quam invisibilium. Filius est Verbum, Sapientia, & Imago Patris. Spiritus Sanctus est æterna [atque essentialis] potentia & virtus procedens à Patre & à Filio. Ita tamen ut hæc distinctio non efficiat ut Deus sit veluti in tres partes divisus: quandoquidem Scriptura nos docet, Patrem, & Filium, & Spiritum Sanctum suam quidem singulos habere hypostasin seu subsistentiam proprietatibus suis distinctam: ita tamen ut tres hæ Personæ sint tantùm unus & solus Deus. 2. Certum igitur est Patrem non esse Filium, nec Filium esse Patrem, neque Spiritum Sanctum esse aut Patrem aut Filium. Interim tamen Personæ illæ sic distinctæ, neque sunt divisæ, neque confusæ, neque permixtæ. Neque enim Pater carnem humanam assumpsit, nec Spiritus Sanctus, sed solus Filius. Pater nunquam sine Filio suo fuit, nec sine Spiritu suo Sancto, quia singuli in una eademeâdemque essentiâ ejusdem sunt æternitatis. Nullus ex his aut primus aut ultimus est, quia omnes tres unum sunt in veritate & potentiâ, in bonitate & misericordiâ.
units.tr: In accordance with this truth and this Word of God, we believe in one only God, who is one and eternal essence, distinct in reality, truly and from eternity, into three Persons, each of whom has his own incommunicable properties, namely the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. 1. The Father is the cause, origin, and beginning of all things, both visible and invisible. The Son is the Word, the Wisdom, and the Image of the Father. The Holy Spirit is the eternal [and essential] power and virtue proceeding from the Father and from the Son. Yet this distinction does not make God as if divided into three parts; for Scripture teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit each has his own hypostasis or subsistence, distinguished by its properties, and yet these three Persons are only one and the same God. 2. It is certain, therefore, that the Father is not the Son, nor the Son the Father, nor is the Holy Spirit either the Father or the Son. Yet these Persons, so distinguished, are neither divided, nor confused, nor mixed together. For the Father did not assume human flesh, nor did the Holy Spirit, but the Son alone. The Father was never without his Son, nor without his Holy Spirit, since each of them is of the same eternity in one and the same essence. None of them is first or last, since all three are one in truth and power, in goodness and mercy.

units.la: Contra hunc Articulum doceri videtur.
units.tr: It seems to be taught against this article.

units.la: I. Dogma de Trinitate Personarum in unâ DEI essentiâ, non tantum sensui communi, sed etiam divinis testimonijs aperte adversari.
