units.tr: I. The dogma of the Trinity of Persons in the one essence of God is clearly opposed not only to common sense but also to the divine testimonies.

units.la: Ab HENR. WELSINGIO. Libello de Offic.hom.Christ. sol. C.3. Evangelici una cum Pontificijs, non minus evidenter, quam vehementer errant, quod non Patrem tantum Domini nostri IESU Christi, illum unum DEUM nostrum, cœli terræque Creatorem esse, credunt, sed etiam ipsum IESUM Christum, seu DEI Filium, nec non & Spiritum Sanctum eundem illum unum DEUM esse statuunt. Quod non modo cum ipso sensu communi, ut ipsimet fateri tandem coguntur, manifestè pugnat, sed divinis testimonijs aperte adversatur.
units.tr: From HENRICUS WELSINGIUS, in his little book On the Duties of a Christian Man, sol. C.3. Evangelicals, together with the Papists, err no less plainly than vehemently in believing that not only the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, that one God of ours, the Creator of heaven and earth, but also Jesus Christ himself, the Son of God, and likewise the Holy Spirit, is that same one God. This not only clearly contradicts common sense itself, as they are at last forced to admit, but is clearly opposed to the divine testimonies.

units.la: Ibidem. sol. C.3. Pugnant hæc inter se, illum DEUM nostrum, cœli terræque Creatorem esse unum tantum numero, & tres esse, quorum unusquisque sit ille DEUS noster. Item. Tres vel etiam duæ personæ esse nequeunt, ubi est una tantum numero sive individua essentia, sed ad plures unâ personas constituendas, plures etiam unâ individuæ essentiæ requiruntur.
units.tr: Ibidem, sol. C.3. These things are inconsistent with each other: that our God, the Creator of heaven and earth, is one only in number, and yet that there are three, each of whom is that God of ours. Likewise: Three or even two persons cannot exist where there is only one numerically single or individual essence; for several persons to be constituted, several things of one individual essence are required.

units.la: II. Singulas Personas divinas habere propriam suam Essentiam.
units.tr: II. The individual divine Persons have each their own essence.

units.la: A CORN. VORSTIO, Disp.de DEO, pag.208. Sunt tres saltem, si non plures diversæ res in DEO. Et contradictio quædam videtur esse, rem ullam veré existere, quæ non habeat suam quandam propriam essentiam,
units.tr: From CORNELIUS VORSTIUS, Disputation on God, p. 208. There are at least three, if not more, different things in God. And it seems to be a kind of contradiction for any thing to exist truly which does not have its own essence of some kind.

units.la: ARTICULUS IX. De SS. Trinitate.
units.tr: ARTICLE IX. Concerning the Most Holy Trinity.

units.la: HÆc vero omnia cognoscimus tam ex Sacræ Scripturæ Testimonijs, quam ex Effectis, ijs potissimum, quæ nos in nobismet ipsis sentimus. Et sacræ quidem Scripturæ Testimonia, quæ nos docent sacram hanc Trinitatem credere, passim in Veteri Testamento occurrunt; quæ non tam numeranda, quam certo judicio seligenda sunt. Qualia hæc sunt, Geneseos primo dicit DEVS, Faciamus hominem ad imaginem & similitudinem nostram, &c. Et mox, Creavit itaque DEVS hominem ad imaginem & similitudinem suam, marem, inquam, & fœminam creavit eos. Item, Ecce Adam tanquam unus nostrum factus est. Ex eo enim quod dicitur, Faciamus hominem ad similitudinem nostram, apparet pluralitatem esse Personarum in Deitate. Quum autem dicitur, DEVS creavit, &c. indicatur unitas Divinitatis. Verum quidem est hic non exprimi, quot sint per-sonæ: tamen quod in Veteri Testamento obscuobscurè traditum est, id in Novo nobis clarè admodùm exponitur. Cum enim Dominus noster IEsvs Christus in Iordane bapti-zaretur, Patris vox audita est dicentis, Hic est Filius meus dilectus: & Filius ipse in aquis est visus: Spiritus vero Sanctus sub specie columbæ apparuit. [An non igitur tres sunt?] In communi omnium fidelium Baptismo hæc formula à Christo instituta est: Baptizate omnes gentes in nomine Patris & Filij & Spiritus Sancti. Sic etiam in Evangelio Lucæ, Angelus Gabriel, Mariam Domini nostri matrem alloquitur: Spiritus Sanctus superveniet in te, & virtus Altissimi inumbrabit te, propterea id quod nascetur ex te sanctum, vocabi-tur Filius Dei. [Videmus hic nominari Patrem Altissimum, postea Filium Dei, qui ex Virgine natus est, & Spiritum Sanctum, qui Virginem inumbravit.] Item, Gratia Domini nostri IEsv Christi, & charitas Dei, & communicatio Spiritus Sancti sit vobiscum. [Atque hic videmus clare tres nominari.] Item, Tres sunt qui testificantur in cœlo, Pater, Sermo, & Spiritus Sanctus, & hi tres unum sunt. Qui-bus omnibus locis plenissimè docemur in unico DEo tres esse Personas. 1. Etsi autem hæc doctrina omnem humani ingenij ca-ptum superet, illam tamen nunc ex verbo DEi firmiter credimus, expectantes donec in coelo plene illius cognitione fruamur. Notanda porro sunt etiam harum trium Personarum singularia officia & effecta, quæ erga nos singulæ exerunt. Pater enim voca-tur Creator noster per virtutem ipsius; Filius noster Servator per sanguinem ipsius, Spiritus Sanctus est Sanctificator noster per inhabitationem ipsius in cordibus nostris.
units.tr: We know all these things both from the testimonies of Holy Scripture and from its effects, especially those which we feel within ourselves. The testimonies of Holy Scripture which teach us to believe this holy Trinity occur throughout the Old Testament; they are to be chosen by sound judgement rather than merely counted. Of this kind is the statement at the beginning of Genesis: GOD said, Let us make man in our image and likeness, etc. And soon after: So God created man in his own image and likeness; male, I say, and female he created them. Likewise: Behold, Adam has become as one of us. For from the words, Let us make man in our likeness, it appears that there is a plurality of Persons in the Godhead; but when it is said that GOD created, etc., the unity of the Godhead is indicated. It is true that here it is not expressed how many persons there are; yet what is taught obscurely in the Old Testament is set out for us very clearly in the New. For when our Lord Jesus Christ was baptized in the Jordan, the voice of the Father was heard saying, This is my beloved Son; the Son himself was seen in the waters; and the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove. [Are there not therefore three?] In the common baptism of all believers this formula was instituted by Christ: Baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. So also in the Gospel of Luke the angel Gabriel addresses Mary, the mother of our Lord: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born of you will be called the Son of God. [Here we see the Father named as the Most High, then the Son of God, who was born of the Virgin, and the Holy Spirit, who overshadowed the Virgin.] Likewise: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all. [And here we clearly see three named.] Likewise: There are three who bear witness in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one. From all these passages we are most fully taught that in the one God there are three Persons. 1. Although this doctrine surpasses the grasp of every human mind, nevertheless we now firmly believe it from the Word of God, waiting until we enjoy its full knowledge in heaven. Moreover, the particular offices and effects of these three Persons, which each one exercises towards us, are also to be noted. For the Father is called our Creator through his power; the Son our Saviour through his blood; the Holy Spirit is our Sanctifier through his indwelling in our hearts.

units.la: Atque hanc de SS. Trinitate doctrinam jam inde ab Apostolorum ætate ad hæc usque tempora semper vera retinuit Ecclesia, & ad-versus Judæos, Mahumetanos, aliosque pseu-dochristianos & hæreticos defendit, quales fuerunt Marcion, Manes, Praxeas, Sabellius, Samosatenus, [Arius] & similes, qui omnes jure meritóque ab orthodoxis Patribus con-demnati sunt. Recipimus itaque libenter hic tria illa Symbola, nempe Apostolorum, Nice-num & Athanasij, & quæcunque de hoc do-gmate juxta illorum Symbolorum senten-tiam [sacra Concilia] statuerunt.
units.tr: This doctrine of the Most Holy Trinity the Church has always held to be true from the age of the Apostles down to the present times, and has defended it against the Jews, the Muslims, and other pseudo-Christians and heretics, such as Marcion, Manes, Praxeas, Sabellius, Samosatenus, [Arius] and others like them, all of whom were rightly and deservedly condemned by the orthodox Fathers. We therefore gladly receive here those three creeds, namely the Apostles', the Nicene and the Athanasian, and whatever [holy councils] have decided on this doctrine in agreement with the sense of those creeds.

units.la: Contra hunc Articulum doceri videtur.
units.tr: It seems to be taught against this article.

units.la: I. Nulla extare testimonia in S. Scriptura, quibus Trinitas Personarum in Deitate probari possit.
units.tr: I. There are no testimonies in Holy Scripture by which the Trinity of Persons in the Godhead can be proved.

units.la: Ab H. Welsingio, Lib. de Off. hom. Christ. sol. C. 4.
units.tr: From H. Welsingius, Book on the Duties of a Christian Man, sol. C. 4.

units.la: Perquirant Evangelici Scripturas quamdiu velint, nunquā dogma istud de Trinitate in illis expressum invenient. Sed neque vel aperte vel obscure id colligi deprehendent. Quinimò ( ut interim de Scripturæ testimonijs dogma istud aperte damnantibus aliquid explicatius dicamus) plané contrariam sententiam in S. literis consignatam reperient.
units.tr: Let the Evangelicals search the Scriptures as long as they like; they will never find this dogma of the Trinity expressed in them. Nor will they discover that it can be gathered from them either plainly or obscurely. Indeed (so that, meanwhile, we may say something more explicit about the testimonies of Scripture which clearly condemn this dogma) they will find in the holy writings a plainly contrary opinion set down.

units.la: ARTICULUS X. De aeterna Deitate Filii Dei, Domini nostri Iesu Christi.
units.tr: ARTICLE X. Of the eternal Deity of the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: CRedimus IESVM CHRISTVM respectu naturæ ipsius divinæ, esse unicum Dei Filium, 1. ab æterno genitum, 2. non factum aut creatum, sic enim esset creatura, sed Patri ὁμοούσιον καὶ συναΐδιον, seu ejusdem cum Patre essentiæ, eique coæternum, characterem, seu veram imaginem, ὑποστάσεως[?] Patris & splendorem gloriæ ejus, in omnibus [& per omnia] ei æqualem. 3. Est autem is Filius Dei non tantum ab eo tempore, quo naturam no-stram stram humanam induit, sed ab æterno, uti haec testimonia inter se collata nos docent. Moses ait DEVM creasse mundum: At divus Iohannes per Sermonem, quem DEVM vocat, omnia facta fuisse dicit. [Et quem D. Ioannes Sermonem vocat, eundem D. Paulus Filium vocat] asserens, DEVM per Filium suum saecula seu mundum condidisse. [Præterea docet D.Paulus DEVM omnia per IESVM Christum creasse.]
units.tr: We believe that JESUS CHRIST, with respect to his divine nature itself, is the unique Son of God: (1) begotten from eternity, (2) not made or created (for then he would be a creature), but homoousios and coeternal with the Father [ὁμοούσιον καὶ συναΐδιον], that is, of the same essence as the Father and coeternal with him, the character, or true image, of the substance [ὑποστάσεως] of the Father and the splendour of his glory, equal to him in all things [and through all things]. (3) This Son of God is not only from the time when he put on our human nature, but from eternity, as these testimonies compared with one another teach us. Moses says that God created the world; but the divine John, calling him the Word, says that all things were made through the Word, asserting that God made the ages, or the world, through his Son. Furthermore, the apostle Paul teaches that God created all things through Jesus Christ.

units.la: 4. Sequitur itaque cum, qui & DEVS, & Sermo, & Filius, & IESVS Christus dicitur, jam tum extitisse, quum ab ipso omnia condita fuerunt. Idcirco Michæas Propheta inquit, Exitus ejus ab initio, à diebus æternitatis. Item, [Est primogenitus omnis creaturæ] &c, Est absque initio dierum, & absque fine vitæ. [Psalmo secundo, Filius meus es, ego hodie genui te: Osculamini Filium.] Est igitur ille verus & æternus DEVS, omnipotens ille, quem invocamus, adoramus, & colimus, 5. [omnibus diebus vitæ nostræ.]
units.tr: (4) It follows, then, that he who is called God, and Word, and Son, and Jesus Christ, already existed when all things were made by him. Therefore the prophet Micah says, "His goings forth are from the beginning, from the days of eternity." Likewise, "He is the firstborn of every creature," etc. "He is without beginning of days and without end of life." [In Psalm 2, "You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Kiss the Son."] He is therefore that true and eternal God, the almighty one whom we call upon, adore and worship (5) all the days of our life.

units.la: Contra hunc Articulum doceri videtur.
units.tr: Against this article the following is taught.

units.la: 1. IESVM Christum non vocari Filium Dei, respectu naturæ ipsius divinæ.
units.tr: 1. That Jesus Christ is not called the Son of God with respect to his divine nature itself.

units.la: Ab HENR. WELSINGIO, De offic. hom. Christ. sol. D.1. Sequitur hominem illum e ISUM Nazarenum sine ulla divina cujusdam alterius essentia, quam ipse habeat, consideratione, esse unicum Dei Filium.
units.tr: From Henry Welsing, On the Office of the Christian Man, solution D.1. It follows that that man Jesus of Nazareth, without any other divine essence which he might have, apart from consideration, is the unique Son of God.

units.la: Ibidem. sol. D.2. Concludendum est igitur Filium Dei unigenitum non esse substantiam quandam divinam, ex ipsâ substantiâ Dei genitam, quæ humanam naturam induerit.
units.tr: Ibidem, solution D.2. It must therefore be concluded that the only-begotten Son of God is not a certain divine substance, begotten from the very substance of God, which put on human nature.

units.la: A VORSTIO, Disp. de DEO, pag. 432. Christus qua homo est, & qua Mediator à Deo constitutus, hoc respectu etiam unicus & singularissimus Dei Filius appellari debet.
units.tr: From Conrad Vorstius, Disputation on God, p. 432. Christ, as man and as Mediator appointed by God, must also in this respect be called the unique and most singular Son of God.

units.la: II. Christum appellari DEI Filium, non quod ab æterno à Patre sit genitus, sed propter ejus in tempore ortum seu nativitatem ex Virgine, resurrectionem, & personæ regiæ seu muneris excellentiam.
units.tr: II. Christ is called the Son of God not because he was begotten by the Father from eternity, but on account of his origin or birth in time from the Virgin, his resurrection, and the excellence of his royal person and office.

units.la: A WELSINGIO, De Offic. hom. Christ. sol. C. 7. Nihil apud sacros autores legimus, quod nobis persuadere queat, aut saltem innuere, DEUM ex suâ substantiâ generare. Quod enim Psalm 2. 7. dicitur, Ego hodie genui te, id non ad æternam aliquam generationem (unde saltem consequenter illa substantialis, ut sic dicam, generatio elici posset) sed ad eam quæ in tempore, ut loquuntur, & nominatim respectu Christi, in die Resurrectionis facta est, referri debere, cum alia multa, tum præsertim loca illa Act. 13.33. Rom. 1. 4. Satis evidenter ostendunt.
units.tr: From Welsing, On the Office, solution C.7. We read nothing in the sacred authors that could persuade us, or even hint, that God begets from his own substance. For what is said in Psalm 2:7, "Today I have begotten you," refers not to some eternal generation (from which at least by consequence that substantial, so to speak, generation could be drawn), but to that which took place in time, as they say, and specifically with respect to Christ, on the day of the Resurrection. Many other passages, and especially Acts 13:33 and Romans 1:4, show this quite clearly.

units.la: Ibidem. Cur IESUS Christus DEI Filius appelletur, nempe unicus & singularis ille Dei filius, duplex est causa, altera, videlicet, quæ ad ejus ortum & nativitatem pertinet: altera, quæ ejusdem dignitatem, & personæ, quam sustinet, excellentiam respicit, sine ulla ipsius essentiæ quæ aliorum filiorum DEI essentiâ præstantior. ab eâve di-versa sit, vel mentione vel consideratione.
units.tr: Ibidem. There are two causes why Jesus Christ is called the Son of God, namely that unique and singular Son of God. One is which pertains to his origin and birth. The other regards the excellence of his dignity and of the person he sustains, and the excellence of that person, without any essence of his more excellent than the essence of the other sons of God, or different from it, either in mention or in consideration.

units.la: Ibidem.sol. C. 8. Priorem causam expressit ipse Angelus Gabriel, inquiens ipsi virgini, mox IESU Christi futuræ matri, Luc. 1. SS. Spiritus S. superveniet te, & virtus altissimi inumbrabit te , ideoq; quod ex te nascetur, vocabitur Filius Dei. Vides modum conceptionis & primam existentia illius hominis Jesu Nazareni causam esse, ut ipse homo Jesus Nazarenus, qui Christus est, Dei Filius appelletur, & quidem consequenter singularis sive unicus, & unigenitus Dei Filius, quandoquidem nemo alius unquam talem a Deo sui ipsius originem & generationem habuit. Ibidem. Vides hic rursus hominis illius Jesu Nazareni, summam post Deum dignitatem, & regiae personae, quam in ipso Dei populo sustinet, omnium maximam excellentiam causam esse, cur sit ille unicus & singularis Dei Filius.
units.tr: Ibidem, solution C.8. The angel Gabriel himself expressed the first cause, saying to the Virgin, soon to be the mother of Jesus Christ, Luke 1: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore that which will be born of you will be called the Son of God." You see that the manner of conception and the first existence of that man Jesus of Nazareth is the cause why the man Jesus of Nazareth, who is Christ, should be called the Son of God, and indeed consequently the singular, or unique, and only-begotten Son of God, since no one else ever had such an origin and generation from God. Ibidem. You see here again that the highest dignity after God, and the royal person which he sustains among God's own people, is the greatest excellence and the cause why he is the unique and singular Son of God.

units.la: Ibidem.sol.D.1. Ipse Christus satis aperte docuit, idem esse in ipso, quòd sit Christus, & quod sit Filius Dei, cum Joan.10.36. Judaeis ostendens, cur se appellasset Dei Filium, rationem attulit, quod Pater ipsum sanctificasset, & in mundum misisset.
units.tr: Ibidem, solution D.1. Christ himself taught quite plainly that being Christ and being the Son of God are the same in him, when, showing the Jews why he had called himself the Son of God, citing John 10:36, he gave as the reason that the Father had sanctified him and sent him into the world.

units.la: A CONR. VORSTIO. Lib. de Filiatione Christi, pag. 19.
units.tr: From Conrad Vorstius, On the Sonship of Christ, p. 19.

units.la: Nullo pacto fieri potest, ut DEVS aliquem ex suâ substan-tiâ generet.
units.tr: In no way is it possible for God to beget anyone from his own substance.

units.la: Ibidem.pag.37. Aeterna & ineffabilis generatio Filii ex sub-stantia Patris neque sacris literis explicatur.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 37. The eternal and ineffable generation of the Son from the substance of the Father is not explained in the sacred letters.

units.la: Ibidem. In Christo homine triplex divina Filiatio, seu ex Deo generatio observanda est. Prima pertinet ad ho-minis Christi ortum. Secunda ad sanctificationem, sive un-ctionem illam divinam, qua etiam tum, cum mortalis homo esset, a Deo instructus fuit. Tertia ad gloriosam re-surrectionem.
units.tr: Ibid. In Christ as man, a threefold divine sonship, or generation from God, is to be observed. The first pertains to the origin of the man Christ. The second pertains to his sanctification, or that divine anointing, by which he was instructed by God even while he was a mortal man. The third pertains to his glorious resurrection.

units.la: Ibidem. pag. 44. De prima Filiatione inquit Angelus: Luc.1.35.[?] Propterea quod virtus altissimi te inumbrabit, &c: Ibidem. pag. 49. De secunda Filiatione sua divina ipse Christus disserit Ioan. 10.35.36. Si illos dixit Deos &c. quibus verbis significat Christus se propterea merito vocari Filium Dei, quia sit a Patre suo sanctificatus, hoc est, Spiritum S. copiose nactus, & cum divino imperio ac potestate in mundum missus ad servandum genus hu-manum.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 44. Concerning the first sonship the angel says: Luke 1:35, "Because the power of the Most High will overshadow you," etc. Ibid., p. 49. Concerning the second, his divine sonship, Christ himself speaks in John 10:35–36, "If he called them gods," etc. By these words Christ signifies that he is rightly called the Son of God because he has been sanctified by his Father, that is, has abundantly received the Holy Spirit and was sent into the world with divine authority and power to save the human race.

units.la: Ibidem. pag. 59. De postrema eaque perfectissima Christi hominis Filiatione divina disserit Apostolus, Act.13.32.33. Ubi docet Christum à Deo fuisse resuscitatum à mortuis, atque ita impletum illud Psalm.2.7.Et pag.64. Neque desunt, qui locum Rom.1.4. ita exponant, ut doceant Christum hominem juxta carnem mortalem, natura quidem ex semine Davidis esse factum: juxta Spiritum vero, quo fuit à Patre sanctificatus, Filium Dei esse definitum, seu definita aut perfecta quadam ratione factum, nempe per resurrectionem è mortuis.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 59. Concerning the last and most perfect divine sonship of the man Christ, the Apostle speaks in Acts 13:32–33, where he teaches that Christ was raised from the dead by God, and so that saying of Psalm 2:7 was fulfilled. And p. 64. Nor are there lacking those who expound Rom. 1:4 in such a way as to teach that Christ as man, according to the mortal flesh, was indeed made by nature from the seed of David, but according to the Spirit, by which he was sanctified by the Father, was defined to be the Son of God, or was made so in a certain defined or perfect manner, namely by the resurrection from the dead.

units.la: III. Filium Dei secundum Deitatem suam non esse Patri æqualem.
units.tr: III. That the Son of God according to his Deity is not equal to the Father.

units.la: A Conr. Vorstio, Disp.de Deo, pag.185. Scriptu-ræ Patri suam prærogativam semper afferre solent, præsertim ubi conjunctam illius simul & Christi mentionem faciunt. Exempli gratia Joan.1.1. dicitur cum articulo, Et sermo erat apud τὸν Θεόν videlicet Patrem, qui κατ' ἐξοχὴν solet appellari Deus. Verum statim de Christo subjicitur, Et sermo erat Θεὸς, absque articulo.
units.tr: From Conrad Vorstius, Disp. on God, p. 185. The Scriptures usually add the Father's prerogative always, especially where they mention him together with Christ. For example, in John 1:1 it is said with the article, "and the Word was with the God [τὸν Θεόν]", namely the Father, who is commonly called God par excellence [κατ' ἐξοχὴν]. But straightway of Christ it is added, "and the Word was God [Θεὸς]", without the article.

units.la: Ibidem.pag.179. In N.T. quoties Dei Patris simul & Christi mentio fit, toties Pater κατ' ἐξοχὴν Deus, Filius autem Dominus appellatur: qui propterea etiam alibi Christus Domini seu Jehovæ, vel Christus Dei appellatur, ut subordinatio ejus ad Deum Patrem, à quo totus ipse pendet, obiter hac phrasi indicetur.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 179. In the New Testament, as often as mention is made of God the Father together with Christ, the Father is called God par excellence [κατ' ἐξοχὴν], but the Son is called Lord. For this reason Christ is also elsewhere called Christ of the Lord or of Jehovah, or Christ of God, so that his subordination to God the Father, on whom he wholly depends, is incidentally indicated by this phrase.

units.la: A Welsingio, de Offic.hom. Christ.sol.C.5. Quod si loca pene innumerabilia, in quibus Christus ab illo uno Deo distinguitur, non satis sint ad persuadendum unicuique, Christum non esse illum unum Deum, certè illud satis superque esse debet, quod Jesus Christus illius unius Dei Filius passim appellatur. Articulus enim in Græco nomini Dei additus unum illum Deum significandi vim habet. Quare si Christus unius illius Dei Filius est, nullâ ratione fieri potest, ut ipse Christus sit unus ille DEVS.
units.tr: From Welsingius, On the Office of the Christian Man, chap. 5. But if the almost countless passages in which Christ is distinguished from that one God are not enough to persuade anyone that Christ is not that one God, then surely this must be enough and more than enough: that Jesus Christ is everywhere called the Son of that one God. For the article in Greek, added to the name of God, has the force of signifying that one God. Therefore, if Christ is the Son of that one God, it can by no means be the case that Christ himself is that one God.

units.la: Ab ADOL. VENATORE, contra Pasl.[?] Dord.pag. 57. 58. 59.
units.tr: From Adolph Venator, against [Pasl.?] Dord., pp. 57, 58, 59.

units.la: Existimo neminem debere constringi, ut in doctrinâ de Deitate IESV Christi, agnoscat vocem ὁμοούσιον, Nam vox hæc primum conficta fuit in Concilio Niceno, in quo Episcopi, qui hanc vocem ibi decreverunt, in duobus apertissimè errarunt: Primum erat quod hi egregij, si Dijs placet, Episcopi decreverant, non licere Ministris verbi divini per omnem vitam suam unquam uxores ducere.
units.tr: I think no one ought to be compelled, in the doctrine of the Deity of Jesus Christ, to acknowledge the word homoousion [ὁμοούσιον]. For this word was first contrived at the Council of Nicaea, at which the bishops who decreed this word there plainly erred in two respects. The first was that these excellent bishops, if you please, decreed that ministers of the divine Word may never take wives at any time in their whole life.

units.la: Alterum, quod ut confessioni de hac voce ὁμοούσιον ab ipsis decretæ, fidem aliquam facerent, eandem imposuerint sepulchris duorum Episcoporum defunctorum, cum invocatione ad defunctos illos facta, ut huic confessioni in signum & testimonium veritatis cum ipsis subscribere vellent. Et postero mane reversos ipsos invenisse confessionem hanc, quam obsignatam sepulchro imposuerant, duorum istorum Episcoporum manibus subsignatam. Niceph.Hist.Eccl.l.8.c.23.
units.tr: The second was that, in order to give some credibility to the confession about this word homoousion which they had drawn up, they placed it upon the tombs of two deceased bishops, with an invocation made to those dead men, so that they would wish to subscribe to this confession along with them as a sign and testimony of the truth. And returning the next morning, they found this confession, which they had placed sealed upon the tomb, subscribed by the hands of those two bishops. Nicephorus, Ecclesiastical History, bk. 8, chap. 23.

units.la: Ibidem.pag.61. Nolo etiam Constantini sententiam improbare, cum existimaret Alexandrum & Arium in pace potuisse manere, & unitatem fidei servare, utrumque in sententiâ suâ persistentem, nec necesse fuisse ut hac de re contenderetur, sed fuisse tantum subtilitates quasdam minimè necessarias, de quibus inter ipsos contendebatur. Euseb. in vita Constant.lib.2.cap.63.&seqq.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 61. Nor do I wish to disapprove of the opinion of Constantine, since he thought that Alexander and Arius could have remained in peace and kept the unity of faith, each persisting in his own opinion, and that it was not necessary to contend about this matter, but that there were only certain minor subtleties, not at all necessary, about which they were disputing. Eusebius, Life of Constantine, bk. 2, chap. 63 and following.

units.la: Theol. mera & vera prafat. pag. 24. 25. Celeberrimum primum Concilium, quod in Christianitate publicâ, magno cum apparatu, est celebratum, fuit Concilium Nicenum,in quo multi fuerunt abusus, & nulla alia miracula facta, quam hoc sequens, quod describit Nicephorus, lib. 8. c. 23. &c. An poterant Episcopi, qui Symbolum hoc de Deitate IESV, & de articulo de Trinitate ita composuerant & concluserant, hoc uti medio, quod in Scripturis tam rigidè vetatur? Theol. mera & vera, pag. 24. 25. Quæst. An ergo Iesvs unum est cum Patre? Resp. Ita ipse loquitur apud Ioannem Evangelistam, cap. 10. ꝟ. 30. Ego & pater unum sumus. Quæst. An voluntas Iesv semper una fuit cum voluntate Patris? & an unquam illi repugnavit? Resp. Ille semper unus erat voluntate cum Patre. Quæst. Cum passurus erat, an tum unus erat cum Patre, & voluntatem suam Dei voluntati subjiciebat? Resp. Patet idipsum ex ipsius precatione Marc. 14. 36. Quæst. An non omnes quoque fideles unum esse debent cum Deo, & cum Iesv, idem sentire, & eandem habere voluntatem? Resp. Omninò hoc necessarium est: &c. Quæst. Explica mihi totam seriem, quomodo nos unum cum Deo, & naturæ ipsius participes fiamus? Resp. Idipsum nobis egregiè describit Apostolus Petrus, 1. Epist. cap. 1. à ꝟ. 2. ad 12.
units.tr: Theology Pure and True, preface, pp. 24, 25. The very famous first council, which was held in public Christendom with great pomp, was the Council of Nicaea, in which there were many abuses, and no other miracles were performed than the following, which Nicephorus describes in bk. 8, chap. 23 etc. Could the bishops, who had so composed and concluded this creed concerning the Deity of Jesus and the article concerning the Trinity, use as a means this thing which is so strictly forbidden in the Scriptures? Theology Pure and True, pp. 24, 25. Question: Is Jesus therefore one with the Father? Answer: He himself speaks thus in John the Evangelist, chap. 10, v. 30: "I and the Father are one." Question: Was the will of Jesus always one with the will of the Father, and did it ever oppose him? Answer: He was always one in will with the Father. Question: When he was about to suffer, was he then one with the Father, and did he subject his will to the will of God? Answer: This is plain from his own prayer, Mark 14:36. Question: Ought not all the faithful also to be one with God and with Jesus, to think the same and to have the same will? Answer: This is altogether necessary, etc. Question: Explain to me the whole sequence, how we may become one with God and partakers of his nature. Answer: The Apostle Peter describes this very well for us, 1 Epistle, chap. 1, from v. 2 to 12.

units.la: Ab ARMINIO Declar. ad Ord. Holl. p. 64. Nullo modo tanquam bene dictum excusari potest, Filium Dei αὐτοθεὸν esse.
units.tr: From Arminius, Declaration to the Holland Estates, p. 64. It cannot in any way be excused as a well-spoken statement that the Son of God is autotheos [αὐτοθεὸν].

units.la: A P TRO CVPO, contra Smout. pag. 56. Non est doctrina hæretica, neque unquam in quoquam damnata, docere Filium Dei non esse αὐτοθεόν.
units.tr: From P. Trocupus, against Smout, p. 56. It is not a heretical doctrine, nor one ever condemned in anyone, to teach that the Son of God is not autotheos [αὐτοθεόν].

units.la: A S. EPISCOPIO, Disput. privat. 11. corol. 3. An Filius sit αὐτοθεός? Distingui quidem posse, sed propter periculum abstinendum putamus.
units.tr: From S. Episcopius, Private Disputation 11, corollary 3. Is the Son autotheos [αὐτοθεός]? We think the question can indeed be distinguished, but on account of the danger we think it should be avoided.

units.la: Notandum est hic diligenter, quod etiam VORSTIVS bene docet, Disput. de Causis defer. Pap. 22. Thes. 10. eos qui negant Christum respectu essentiæ divinæ αὐτοθέον recte vocari, non posse statuere Christum, quoad absolutam Deitatis essentiam, esse hunc ipsum unum numero DEVM, qui prorsus sit independens.
units.tr: It must be noted carefully here that Vorstius also teaches well, Disp. on the Causes of the Deferring of the Papists, p. 22, thesis 10, that those who deny that Christ is rightly called autotheos [αὐτοθέον] with respect to the divine essence cannot hold that Christ, as to the absolute essence of the Deity, is this very one God in number, who is wholly independent.

units.la: IV. Ex opere creationis, quod Filio attribuitur, non posse probari ejus æternam Deitatem.
units.tr: IV. That the eternal Deity of the Son cannot be proved from the work of creation, which is attributed to him.

units.la: A VORSTIO, Disput. de Deo, pag. 125. Quod Zanchius ex eo colligit æternitatem Dei, quod Heb. 1. 2. & 11. 3. dicitur ipse secula condidisse: non satis solidum est argumentum: cum per absolutam Dei potentiam fieri possit, ut qui ipse aliquando ortus est, per donatam Dei virtutem mundum aliquem ex subjecta seu præparata materia constituat, ex quo deinde multa secula ex ordine fluant.
units.tr: From VORSTIUS, Disput. de Deo, p. 125. The argument Zanchius draws from Heb. 1. 2 and 11. 3, that God is said to have made the ages, is not solid enough. By God's absolute power it can happen that one who himself once came into being, by a power given him by God, establishes some world out of matter that is already present or prepared, and from this many ages then follow in order.

units.la: v. IESUM Christum non esse verum & aeternum DEUM.
units.tr: v. That Jesus Christ is not true and eternal God.

units.la: AWELSINGIO, Lib. de Offic. hom. Christ. sol. C.s. Ex quo necessario sequitur, ne ipsum quidem Iesum Christum esse illum DEUM. Ibidem. Quare ne ipse quidem Iesus Christus est ille noster unus DEUS. Ibidem. Fieri non potest, ut ipse Christus sit unus ille DEUS.
units.tr: From WELSINGIUS, Lib. de Offic. hom. Christ. sol. C.s. From this it necessarily follows that Jesus Christ himself is not that God. Ibidem. Therefore Jesus Christ himself is not that one God of ours. Ibidem. It cannot be that Christ himself is that one God.

units.la: Ibidem.pag. C.6. Et satis hæc in præsentiâ esse volumus, ad istum insignem Evangelicorum errorem patefaciendum, dum una cum Pontificijs, statuunt, non solum Iesu Christi Patrem, sed etiam tam Dei Filium, quam Spiritum S. esse illum unum DEUM nostrum, cœli terræque creatorem.
units.tr: Ibidem, p. C.6. We wish to say enough for the present to lay open this notable error of the Evangelicals, namely that, together with the Papists, they hold that not only the Father of Jesus Christ but also the Son of God as well as the Holy Spirit is that one God of ours, the creator of heaven and earth.

units.la: P. CUPUS affirmavit Ioanni Taurino, esse inter Remonstrantes, qui dubitent de æterna Deitate Iesu Christi.
units.tr: P. CUPUS affirmed to John Taurinus that there are among the Remonstrants some who doubt the eternal Deity of Jesus Christ.

units.la: REMONSTRANTES nonnulli palàm professi fuerunt, se in S.Scripturis nullum invenire potuisse argumentum, ex quo æterna Deitas Iesu Christi solidè probari posset.
units.tr: Some Remonstrants openly professed that they could find in the Holy Scriptures no argument from which the eternal Deity of Jesus Christ could be solidly proved.

units.la: ARTICULUS XI. De Persona, & æterna Deitate Spiritus Sancti.
units.tr: ARTICLE XI. On the Person and eternal Deity of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: CRedimus etiam & confitemur Spiri-tum Sanctum à Patre & Filio ab æter-no procedere: itaque nec factum, nec creatum, nec genitum fuisse, sed ab utroque tantum procedentem, qui ordine tertia est Trinitatis Persona, i. ejusdem essentiæ, gloriæ & majestatis cum Patre & Filio. Ideoque & ipse verus & æternus DEVS est. 2.
units.tr: We also believe and confess that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son from eternity; therefore he was neither made, nor created, nor begotten, but proceeds from both alone. He is the third Person of the Trinity in order, that is, of the same essence, glory and majesty with the Father and the Son. Therefore he is also true and eternal God. 2.

units.la: Contra hunc Articulum doceri videtur.
units.tr: It seems that the following is taught against this article.

units.la: I. Spiritum Sanctum non esse Personam, sed tantum vim atque efficaciam quandam DEI.
units.tr: I. That the Holy Spirit is not a Person, but only a certain power and efficacy of God.

units.la: Ab HENR. WELSINGIO, De Offic. hom. Christ. sol. D. 3. Effet hic aliquid dicendum de Evangelicorum errore, quod Spiritus S. sit Persona. Ibidem. Hinc sequitur eum ne Per-sonam quidem esse, sed vim atque efficaciam DEI, quâres aliquo modo sanctificantur.
units.tr: By HENRY WELSINGIUS, De Offic. hom. Christ. sol. D. 3. Here something should be said about the error of the Evangelicals, that the Holy Spirit is a Person. Ibidem. From this it follows that he is not even a Person, but a power and efficacy of God, by which the elect are in some way sanctified.

units.la: Ab HENR. SLATIO, Epist. ad N. 9. Mart. A. 1608. Potentia DEI est Spiritus narium & oris DEI, hoc est, est potentia, quam DEVS de se sparsit, postquam in tempore creare cæpit. Cæpit autem creare, cum Spiritum edere, hoc est, spirare inciperet. Et hæc quidem potentia essen-tialis DEI potentia non est, etiamsi procedat ab essentiali potentia; quemadmodum lux Solis origo atque principium est luminis aërij, quo Sol, ceu instrumento, utitur ad omnes suas operationes.
units.tr: By HENRY SLATIUS, Epist. ad N. 9 March 1608. The power of God is the Spirit of the nostrils and mouth of God; that is, it is the power which God poured out from himself when he began in time to create. He began to create when he brought forth the Spirit, that is, when he began to breathe. And this power is not the essential power of God, even if it proceeds from his essential power; just as the light of the sun is the origin and source of atmospheric light, which the sun uses, as an instrument, for all its operations.

units.la: II. Spiritum Sanctum non esse verum ac æternum DEVM, cum Patre & Filio.
units.tr: II. That the Holy Spirit is not the true and eternal God with the Father and the Son.

units.la: Ab HENR. WELSINGIO, Lib. de Off. hom. Christ. sol. C. 6. Et satis hæc in præsentiâ esse volumus, ad istum insignem Evangelicorum errorem patefaciendum, dum, unâ cum Pontificijs, statuunt non solum IESV Christi Patrem, sed etiam tam DEI Filium, quam Spiritum Sanctum esse illum unum DEVM nostrum.
units.tr: From HENRY WELSINGIUS, Lib. de Off. hom. Christ. sol. C. 6. And we wish to say enough for the present to lay open this notable error of the Evangelicals, namely that, together with the Papists, they hold that not only the Father of Jesus Christ, but also the Son of God as well as the Holy Spirit, is that one God of ours, .

units.la: Ibidem. D. 3. Ex quo consequitur, si Spiritus S. non est di-vina ejus essentia persona, ejus vim atque efficaciam esse.
units.tr: Ibidem, D. 3. From this it follows that if the Holy Spirit is not a divine person of his essence, he is only his power and efficacy.

units.la: ARTICULUS XII. De Creatione Mundi: & de Angelis.
units.tr: ARTICLE XII. On the Creation of the World, and on Angels.

units.la: CRedimus Patrem per Verbum suum, hoc est, per Filium coelum, terram, & reliquas creaturas omnes ex nihilo creasse, cum illi visum fuit opportunum, singulisque suum esse, formam, & varia officia tribuisse, ut Creatori suo inservirent. Eumque nunc illas fovere, sustentare, & regere, secundum aeternam suam Providentiam, & per immē-sam virtutem suam. Idque ut illæ quidem Homini, Homo vero DEO suo inserviat.
units.tr: We believe that the Father, through his Word, that is, through the Son, created heaven, earth and all the other creatures out of nothing, when it seemed good to him, and gave to each its own being, form and various offices, so that they might serve their Creator. And that he now cherishes, sustains and governs them according to his eternal providence and by his immeasurable power; so that they serve man, and man serves his God.

units.la: Creavit etiam Angelos, omnes natura bo-nos, ut ministri ipsius essent, & electis etiam inservirent: quorum tamen nonnulli ab excellenti illa natura, in qua eos DEVS creavit, in perditionem aeternam deciderunt: alij vero singulari DEI gratia, in primo illo statu suo perstiterunt. Diaboli quidem & cacodæmones illi ita corrupti & depravati sunt, ut & DEI & omnis boni conjurati sint hostes, qui Ecclesiæ & singulis ipsius membris tanquam prædones è speculâ omnibus viribus insidiantur, ut imposturis suis ac deceptionibus omnia destruant atque pessundent: [atque adeò quidem ut se adorari ab omnibus velint, quem in finem multa hominibus pollicentur: neque mirum hoc est, cum Diabolus Christum ausus fuerit aggredi, eumq; permovere ut ipsum adoraret. ] Idcirco propriâ suâ malitiâ perpetuæ condemnationi addicti, expectant indies horrenda suorum facinorum supplicia ac tormenta. Respuimus itaque atque execramur hoc loco Saducæorum errorem, qui Spiritus ullos aut Angelos esse negarunt. Item & Manichæorum errorem, qui asserunt Diabolos ex seipsis originem ducere, & ex propriâ suâ naturâ malos esse: non autem corruptos per inobedientiam voluntariam.
units.tr: He also created the angels, all good by nature, to be his ministers and to serve the elect as well. Some of them, however, fell from that excellent nature in which God created them into eternal perdition, while others, by the singular grace of God, persevered in their first state. The devils and those evil demons have been so corrupted and depraved that they are sworn enemies of God and of all good. Like robbers from a watchtower, they lie in wait with all their strength for the Church and each of its members, so as to destroy and ruin everything by their deceits and impostures; [and indeed they wish to be worshipped by all, and to this end they promise many things to men. This is no wonder, since the devil dared to attack Christ and to persuade him to worship him.] Therefore, having been condemned to perpetual damnation by their own malice, they daily await the dreadful punishments and torments of their crimes. Accordingly we reject and execrate here the error of the Sadducees, who denied that there are any spirits or angels. Likewise the error of the Manichaeans, who assert that devils derive their origin from themselves and are evil by their own nature, and not corrupted through voluntary disobedience.

units.la: ARTICULUS XIII. De Providentiâ Dei.
units.tr: ARTICLE XIII. Concerning the Providence of God.

units.la: Credimus Deum hunc Opt.Max. post-quam res omnes creasset, eas minimè fortis aut fortunæ arbitrio commisisse, sed ipsummet illas ex præscripto sacrosanctæ suæ voluntatis ita assiduè regere & gubernare, ut nihil in hoc mundo absque illius decreto atque ordinatione contingat : 1. quanquam tamen DEVS malorum,quæ in hoc mundo accidunt, neque auctor, neque reus dici possit.2. Tam latè patet infinita & incomprehensibilis illius tum potentia tum bonitas,ut tunc etiam opera & actiones suas sanctè&justè decernat atq; exequatur,quum & Diabolus & impij injustè agunt. Quæ-cunque verò ille agit,humanum captum excedentia , de ijs nolumus curiosè & supra nostrum captum inquirere: quinimò secreta & justa tamen DEI judicia humiliter & reverenter adoramus. Sufficit enim nobis, quod Christi discipuli esse possimus , & ea duntaxat discamus, quæ ipso verbo suo nos docet, neque hos fines transilire volumus. Hæc verò doctrina immensam nobis adfert consolationem. Ex illâ enim agnoscimus nihil nobis fortuitò contingere, sed omnia Patris nostri cœlestis voluntate, 3. qui pro nobis verâ paternâ curâ excubat, omnia sibi subdisubdita habens, ita ut ne pilus quidem ca-pitis nostri (qui omnes ad unum numerati sunt) evelli, nec minimus passerculus humi cadere, sine Patris nostri voluntate, possit, His itaque penitus acquiescimus, agnoscen-tes DEVM diabolos & inimicos nostros omnes veluti habenis ita frænatos continere, ut sine ipsius voluntate & bona venia, nemini nostrum nocere valeant. Atque hoc loco detestandam Epicuræorum opinionem rejicimus, qui DEVM otiosum, & nihil a-gentem, omniaq; fortunæ & casui committentem finxerunt.
units.tr: We believe that God, the Best and Greatest, after he had created all things, did not leave them to the will of chance or fortune. Rather, by the rule of his most holy will, he constantly governs and directs them, so that nothing in this world happens without his decree and ordinance. (1) Yet God cannot be called the author or the accomplice of the evils that happen in this world. (2) The infinite and incomprehensible power and goodness of God extend so widely that he decrees and carries out his own works and actions in holiness and justice even when the Devil and the wicked act unjustly. As for what he does beyond human understanding, we do not wish to inquire into it with curiosity or beyond our capacity. Rather, we humbly and reverently adore the secret yet just judgments of God. It is enough for us that we can be disciples of Christ, and that we learn only those things which his own Word teaches us; we do not wish to go beyond these limits. This doctrine brings us immense consolation. For from it we recognise that nothing happens to us by chance, but that all things come by the will of our heavenly Father, (3) who watches over us with true fatherly care, holding all things under his control, so that not even a hair of our head (all of which are numbered, one by one) can be plucked out, nor the smallest sparrow fall to the ground, without the will of our Father. Therefore we fully acquiesce in this, acknowledging that God restrains the devil and all our enemies as if with reins, so that they can harm none of us without his will and good permission. Here we also reject the detestable opinion of the Epicureans, who imagined a God who is idle and does nothing, and who leaves all things to fortune and chance.

units.la: Contra hunc Articulum doceri videtur.
units.tr: Against this Article, the following seems to be taught.

units.la: 1. Multa in hoc mundo contingere, quæ non fiant ex decreto atque ordinatione DEI, seu ex præscripto voluntatis suæ.
units.tr: 1. Many things happen in this world which do not come about by the decree and ordinance of God, or by the rule of his will.

units.la: A Con. Vorstio, Disp. de Deo, pag. 64. De voluntate, seu proposito & consilio DEI speciali, non semper ex eventu judicandum est. Multa enim fiunt, quæ DEVS fieri non vult: nec semper fiunt, quæ ipse fieri vult.
units.tr: From Conrad Vorstius, Disputation on God, p. 64. Concerning the will, or the purpose and special counsel, of God, one must not always judge from the outcome. For many things happen which God does not wish to happen; nor do those things always happen which he wishes to happen.

units.la: Ibidem. pag. 65. Legimus DEVM postmodum quædam nolle facere, quæ antea facturum se receperat, imo juraverat: Item velle jam ea facere, adeoque reipsa jam facere, quæ tamen antea minime se facturum prædi-xerat. Item. Non quidquid DEVS vult ab æterno, in æternum vult. Quædam in tempore reipsa vult, quæ antea sic nominatim atque id specie noluit.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 65. We read that God afterwards was unwilling to do certain things which he had earlier undertaken, indeed had sworn, to do. Likewise he now wishes to do those things, and so actually does them, which he had earlier by no means said he would do. Likewise: Not whatever God wills from eternity, he wills for eternity. He actually wills certain things in time which he earlier, by name and in particular, had not willed.

units.la: Ibidem.pag.306. DEI voluntas aliquo modo mutabilis est in ijs,quæ sub conditione vult, vel quæ fieri tantum desi-derat, vel quæ etiam fortassis indefinita prorsus relinquit. Item. Quæ verò indefinita relinquit, de ijs nulla est DEI certa voluntas. Ergo cum hæc à nobis fiunt, non potest dici voluntas ipsius mutata, quippe quæ specialis hic nulla fuit: nulla, inquam, ut fierent vel non fierent præcisè.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 306. The will of God is in some way changeable in those things which he wills under a condition, or which he merely desires to be done, or which perhaps he leaves altogether undetermined. Likewise: Concerning those things which he leaves undetermined, there is no certain will of God. Therefore, when these things are done by us, it cannot be said that his will has changed, since there was no specific will here: none, I say, that they should or should not happen precisely.

units.la: Ibidem.pag.307. Neque enim dubium est, DEVM olim quædam definitè voluisse, quæ jam non ita vult, ac ne velle quidem potest, quo quidem modo tunc voluit: & contrà quædam jam velle, quæ tunc noluit.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 307. For there is no doubt that God once willed certain things definitely, which he now does not so will, nor even can will in the way he then willed; and conversely, now wills certain things which he then did not will.

units.la: Ibidem. Erratur cum ex decreto DEI colligitur, omnia omninò in specie quæcunque in mundo accidunt, similiter ab æterno fuisse à DEO definita.
units.tr: Ibid. People err when they infer from the decree of God that all things whatsoever that happen in the world, down to each particular, were likewise defined by God from eternity.

units.la: Ibidem.pag.108. Si omnia & singula rerum eventa præcisè & ab æterno definita fuissent, nihil opus esset continuâ rerum inspectione & procuratione.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 108. If all and each of the events of things had been precisely and from eternity defined, there would be no need for a continual overseeing and governing of things.

units.la: Ibidem. Constat DEVM in tempore multa facere, quæ antea prædixerat minimè se facturum, & contrà multa nunc omittere, quæ antea facturum se prædixerat. Item. Nec dici potest, ea tantùm, quæ reipsa fiunt, jam olim ab æterno definita esse. Item. DEVS definita sibi fuisse seriò testatur etiam ea, quæ reipsa non fiunt.
units.tr: Ibid. It is evident that God in time does many things which he had earlier said he would by no means do, and conversely now omits many things which he had earlier said he would do. Likewise: Nor can it be said that only those things which actually come about were long ago defined from eternity. Likewise: God seriously testifies that he had defined also those things which in fact do not come about.

units.la: Ibidem.pag.312. Nihil absurdi ex eo sequitur, quod DEVS in tempore quædam præcisè ac definitè velle vel nolle dicitur, quæ fortassis antea non ita præcisè vel voluit vel noluit: quemadmodum nec absurdum est DEVM nunc quædam in specie velle desinere, quæ antea reipsa voluit.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 312. Nothing absurd follows from the fact that God is said to will or not will certain things in time precisely and definitely, which perhaps he earlier did not so precisely will or not will; just as it is not absurd that God should now cease to will in particular certain things which he actually willed earlier.

units.la: Paraphr.pag.4. Quæ DEVS liberè prorsus & contingenter à nobis fieri vult, ea potentius aut efficacius, quam per mo-dum voti & desiderij velle non potest.
units.tr: Paraphrase, p. 4. Those things which God wills to be done by us quite freely and contingently, he cannot will by way of wish and desire more powerfully or effectively.

units.la: Quod DEVS vult ut fiat, hoc efficaciter efficit. Quod vult ut non fiat, hoc efficaciter impedit. Quod neque vult ut fiat, neque vult ut non fiat, hoc permittit creaturæ. Ibidem. pag.121. Ex eventu alicujus rei non potest concludi Deum voluisse ut eveniret.
units.tr: What God wills to happen, this he brings about effectively. What he wills not to happen, this he effectively prevents. What he neither wills to happen nor wills not to happen, this he permits to the creature. Ibid., p. 121. From the outcome of any thing it cannot be concluded that God willed it to come about.

units.la: A SIM. EPISCOPO, Disput. de Volunt. DEI. Thes. 4. Etsi malum aliquod per accidens propter sapientissimam DEI directionem boni occasio fieri aut esse possit, tamen malum ipsum ulla ratione propterea sanctissimum DEUM velle dicendum non est.
units.tr: From Simon Episcopius, Disputation on the Will of God, Thesis 4. Although some evil may by accident become, or be able to become, an occasion of good through the most wise direction of God, nevertheless the evil itself must not on any account be said to be willed by the most holy God.

units.la: Ibidem. Thes. 21. Sanctissimo DEO, summa injustitia & hypocrisis tribui deberet, si arcana voluntate definiret & ordinaret ut fiant ea, quae revelata prohibet, & fieri non vult.
units.tr: Ibid., Thesis 21. Supreme injustice and hypocrisy would be ascribed to the most holy God, if by his secret will he defined and ordained that those things come about which he forbids by revelation and does not wish to happen.

units.la: Disp.privat.6.de Vol.DEI, Corol.5[?]. De volitionibus DEI non est ex eventu judicandum. Item. An non multa fiant, quae DEUS fieri non vellet? Affirmamus.
units.tr: Private disputation 6 on the Will of God, Corollary 5[?]. Concerning the volitions of God, one must not judge from the outcome. Likewise: Do not many things happen which God would not wish to happen? We affirm that they do.

units.la: II. DEUM statui auctorem malorum, quae in mundo accidunt, cum docetur nihil in hoc mundo contingere absque illius decreto atque ordinatione.
units.tr: II. God is made the author of the evils which happen in the world, when it is taught that nothing in this world happens without his decree and ordinance.

units.la: A VORSTIO, Disp. de DEO, pag. 308. Sequeretur DEUM esse auctorem omnium scelerum, si omnia & singula, quaecunque in mundo fiunt, tam mala quam bona jam olim ab omni aeternitate non modo infallibiliter praevisa, sed etiam efficaciter atque absolute à DEO praefinita sunt.
units.tr: From Vorstius, Disputation on God, p. 308. It would follow that God is the author of all crimes, if all and each thing that happens in the world, as much evil as good, had long ago, from all eternity, not only been infallibly foreseen, but also efficaciously and absolutely predetermined by God.

units.la: A IAC. ARMINIO, Contr.Perk.pag.109.110. Bellarminus objicit sententias quorundam Doctorum nostrorum, inde sequi DEUM esse peccati auctorem; DEUM vere peccare; DEUM solum peccare, & peccatum non esse peccatum. Nulla mihi videtur per istam criminationem tuae doctrinae (Perkinse) injuria illata esse.
units.tr: From James Arminius, Against Perkins, pp. 109, 110. Bellarmine objects that from the opinions of certain of our teachers it follows that God is the author of sin; that God truly sins; that God alone sins, and sin is not sin. It seems to me that no injury has been done to your doctrine, Perkins, by this accusation.

units.la: Artic.perpend.pag.15. Doctoribus nostris impingi posse videtur, quod ex ipsorum doctrina sequatur, DEUM au-ctorem esse peccati, quia docent DEUM ordinasse, ut homo peccaret.
units.tr: Articles weighed, p. 15. It seems that it can be charged against our teachers that from their doctrine it follows that God is the author of sin, because they teach that God ordained that man should sin.

units.la: III. Multa, etiam respectu decreti divini, in hoc mundo contingenter, seu fortuito, evenire. A Con: VORSTIO, Disp. de Deo pag. 308. Omnia omninò in specie quaecunque in mundo accidunt, ab aeterno fuisse à DEO definita facilè refellitur, quia sic nulla esset in universo mundo contingentia, nulla quoque arbitrij libertas. Item. DEVS definita sibi fuisse serio testatur, etiam ea quae reipsa non fiunt.
units.tr: III. Many things, even with respect to the divine decree, happen contingently, or by chance, in this world. From Conrad Vorstius, Disputation on God, p. 308. The view that all and each thing whatsoever that happens in the world was from eternity defined by God is easily refuted, because thus there would be no contingency in the whole universe, nor any freedom of choice. Likewise: God seriously testifies that he had defined even those things which in fact do not come about.

units.la: Ibidem. pag. 64. Non semper fiunt quae DEVS fieri vult.
units.tr: Ibid., p. 64. Those things which God wills to happen do not always happen.

units.la: A IAC. ARMINIO, Respons. ad Art. 31. pag. 94. Non modo perperam, sed & imperitè dicitur, rem quae respectu secundarum causarum contingenter fit, respectu decreti divini fieri necessario.
units.tr: From James Arminius, Response to Article 31, p. 94. It is said not only wrongly but also unskilfully that a thing which comes about contingently with respect to secondary causes comes about necessarily with respect to the divine decree.

units.la: Ibidem. pag. 95. Nego quod ossa Christi respectu decreti divini non potuerunt frangi,
units.tr: Ibid., p. 95. I deny that the bones of Christ could not be broken with respect to the divine decree.

units.la: Ibidem. Nihil itaque arbitror à me peccatum esse, quum dixi, Nihil rerum contingentium, hoc est quae contingenter fiunt, seu factae sunt, dici posse necessario fieri vel factum esse respectu decreti divini.
units.tr: Ibid. I think, therefore, that I have sinned in nothing when I said that nothing contingent, that is, what comes about contingently, or has come about, cannot be said to come about necessarily or to have come about necessarily with respect to the divine decree.

units.la: Artic.perpend. pag. 6. Neque benè dictum, Omnia evenire necessario respectu decreti divini.
units.tr: Artic. perpend. p. 6. Nor is it well said that all things happen necessarily with respect to the divine decree.

units.la: Ibidem. pag. 17. Adam non est lapsus ex decreto neque ex ordinatione DEI. Item. Adam non est lapsus necessario, neque decreti, neque ordinationis respectu.
units.tr: Ibid. p. 17. Adam did not fall by decree, nor by the ordinance of God. Likewise: Adam did not fall necessarily, neither with respect to decree nor to ordinance.

units.la: A SIM. EPISCOPIO, Disp. de Pecc. Adami Thes. 18. Neque verò respectus decreti divini quidquam facere nobis videntur ad hoc, ut actus liberi, necessarij etiam dici possint.
units.tr: Simon Episcopius, Disp. de Pecc. Adami, Thes. 18. Indeed, the respect of the divine decree does not seem to us to contribute anything to the point that free acts could also be called necessary.

units.la: ARTICULUS XIV. De Hominis Creatione, Lapsu & Corruptione.
units.tr: ARTICLE XIV. On Man's Creation, Fall and Corruption.

units.la: CRedimus DEVM ex limo terrae hominem ad imaginem suam creasse, bonum,justum,& sanctum [ atque in omnibus plane perfectum, ] qui proprio arbitrio suam voluntatem ad Dei voluntatem componere & conformem reddere possit.1. [ Deus itaque eum creavit constantem duabus partibus, corpore & animâ: corpus e terrâ conditum fuit, Spiritum verò & vitam DEVS ei inspiravit: adeo ut in homine tanta conspiciatur excellentia, ut humanum ingenium illi exprimendæ par non sit. Ejusmodi eum fuisse David testatur, ut nihil illi amplius deesset, quam quod DEVS non esset. Gloria & honore coronatus fuit. ] Verùm cum in honore esset, nescivit, & excellentiam suam non cognovit [jumentis similis factus est: ] sed seipsum sciens & volens peccato, & per consequens morti ac maledictioni subjecit: dum Diaboli verbis, & impofturis aurem præbens, mandatum vitæ transgressus est, quod à Domino acceperat, seq; à DEO, verâ ipsius vitâ per peccatum subduxit atque alienavit, & totam ipsius naturam corrupit ac vitiavit. Quo factum est ut morti tum corporali, tum spirituali sese obnoxium reddiderit, 2. improbus atque perversus effectus fuerit, atque in omnibus vijs & studijs suis corruptus, & præclara illa dona omnia amiserit, quæ à DEO accepe-rat: adeò ut non nisi exiguæ illorum scin-tillæ & vestigia exilia illi relicta sint, quæ sufficiant ad homines reddendos inexcusa-biles, [sed nequaquam ad nos bonos ac DEO probatos efficiendos ]quoniam quidquid in nobis est lucis in cæcas tenebras est conver-sum, ut & Scriptura ipsa docet, dicens, Lux in tenebris lucet, & tenebræ eam non comprehen-derunt. Ibi enim Iohannes manifestè homi-nes tenebras vocat. 3. [ Atque in Psalmo di-citur: Penes te Domine est fons vitæ, & in luce tuâ clarè videmus lucem. ] Idcirco quæcun-que de libero hominis arbitrio [ adversus hæc ] traduntur, ea nos merito rejicimus, quum homo fit servus peccati, nihilque bo-ni ex se possit, nisi datum sit illi de cælo. 4. Quis enim jactare audeat se, quæcunque volue-rit, præstare posse, cum Christus ipse dicat, Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi Pater meus, qui misit me, traxerit eum ? [ D. Paulus testatur naturalem hominem talem esse, qualem Adamus in lapsu suo produxit. ] Quis voluntatem suam ostentet, qui intelligat o-mnes carnis affectus inimicitias esse adversus DEVM? Quis de intelligentiâ suâ gloriabi-tur, qui sciat animalem hominem non esse capacem eorum quæ sunt Spiritus DEI? In summâ, quis vel ullam suam cogitationem in me-dium proferat, qui intelligat nos non esse ido-neos ex nobis ipsis ad cogitandum quidquam, sed quod idonei sumus,id omne ex DEO esse.? 5. [Cogitare minus est quam facere] Certum ergo & firmum manere oportet, quod Apostolus dixit, DEVM esse qui efficit in nobis & ipsum velle, & ipsum efficere, pro gratuitâ suâ benevo-lentiâ. 6. Nulla enim intelligentia, nulla voluntas est menti & voluntati DEI confor-mis, quam Christus in homine non sit o-peratus: quod & ipse nos docet, dicens, Sine me nihil potestis facere. [Christus etiam & hoc dicit, Qui peccatum facit, servus est peccati. Ubi ergo est liberum ejus arbitrium?]
units.tr: We believe that God created man of the clay of the earth in his own image, good, just and holy [and altogether perfect in all things], able by his own free choice to bring his will into agreement with the will of God and to make it conformable to it. [So God created him consisting of two parts, body and soul: the body was formed from the earth, but God breathed into him spirit and life, so that such great excellence is seen in man that human intellect is not equal to expressing it. David testifies that he was of such a kind that nothing was lacking to him except that he was not God. He was crowned with glory and honour.] But when he was in honour, he did not understand it, and did not know his own excellence [he was made like the beasts]; but knowingly and willingly he subjected himself to sin, and consequently to death and curse, when, lending his ear to the words and deceptions of the Devil, he transgressed the command of life that he had received from the Lord, and by sin withdrew and estranged himself from God, his true life, and corrupted and vitiated his whole nature. As a result he made himself liable to death, both bodily and spiritual, became wicked and perverse, and was corrupted in all his ways and pursuits, and lost all those excellent gifts he had received from God; so that only faint sparks of them and small traces remain to him, which suffice to render men inexcusable, [but by no means to make us good and approved before God], since whatever light is in us has been turned into blind darkness, as Scripture itself teaches, saying, The light shines in darkness, and the darkness has not comprehended it. For there John plainly calls men darkness. [And in the Psalm it is said: With you, Lord, is the fountain of life, and in your light we see light clearly.] Therefore, whatever is handed down about man's free will [contrary to these things], we rightly reject, since man is a slave of sin and can do nothing good of himself, unless it be given to him from heaven. For who would dare to boast that he can accomplish whatever he wishes, when Christ himself says, No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him? [The Apostle Paul testifies that natural man is such as Adam produced him in his fall.] Who would display his own will, when he understands that all the affections of the flesh are enmity against God? Who would glory in his own understanding, when he knows that the natural man is not capable of the things of the Spirit of God? In sum, who would put forward any thought of his own, when he understands that we are not competent of ourselves to think anything, but our competence is from God? [To think is less than to do.] It must therefore remain certain and firm, what the Apostle said: that it is God who works in us both to will and to work, for his good pleasure. For no understanding and no will conformable to the mind and will of God is in man which Christ does not work in him; as he himself teaches us, saying, Without me you can do nothing. [Christ also says this: Whoever commits sin is a slave of sin. Where then is his free choice?]

units.la: Contra hunc Articulum doceri videtur.
units.tr: Against this Article the following is apparently taught.

units.la: 1. Hominem non fuisse creatum cum justitia originali, sed ante lapsum etiam habuisse proclivitatem ad peccandum.
units.tr: 1. That man was not created with original righteousness, but even before the fall had a propensity to sin.

units.la: AWELSINGIO, Lib. de Offic. hom. Christ. sol. E.3. dus hujus generis Evangelicæ doctrinæ error sit, quod Adamo ante peccatum justitiam quandam originalem tribuunt, quam, videlicet, simul atque est creatus, ex Dei gratia habuerit.
units.tr: Awelsingius, Lib. de Offic. hom. Christ., sol. E.3. The error of this kind of evangelical doctrine is that they attribute to Adam before sin a certain original righteousness, which, namely, as soon as he was created, he had from the grace of God.

units.la: AIAC. ARMINIO, Artic. perpend. pag. 10. Citra læsionem Dei, Adami, & ipsius veritatis dici potest, Adamum non accepisse neque habuisse in primævo statu potentiam proximam quidvis intelligendi, credendi, faciendi, quod illi intellectu, creditu, facto in quovis statu, ad quem vel suo facto vel Dei dono pervenire potuit, necessarium esse potuit.
units.tr: Aiac. Arminius, Artic. perpend. p. 10. Without injury to God, to Adam, or to the truth itself, it can be said that Adam did not receive, nor have in his primeval state, a proximate power to understand, believe, or do whatever could be necessary for him to understand, believe, or do in any state to which he could have attained either by his own act or by the gift of God.

units.la: Ibidem. pag.18. Inclinatio ad peccandum antea (ante lapsum) in homine fuit, licet non ita vehemens æque & inordinata, ut nunc est.
units.tr: Ibid. p. 18. An inclination to sin existed in man before (before the fall), although not as vehement and disordered as it is now.

units.la: A REMONSTRANTIBVS, Coll.Hag.pag.250. Dona spiritualia ab humana voluntate, in morte spirituali, proprie non separantur, quum illa nunquam in ea fuerint.
units.tr: Remonstrants, Coll. Hag. p. 250. Spiritual gifts are not properly separated from the human will in spiritual death, since they were never in it.

units.la: II. Adamum etiam ante lapsum morti corporali fuisse obnoxium: neque vero demum per peccatum ei obnoxium esse factum.
units.tr: II. That Adam also before the fall was subject to bodily death, and was not made subject to it only through sin.

units.la: A WELSINGIO, De Offic. hom. Christi. pag.E.2. Primum ejusmodi errorem facimus, quod sicuti vulgo ab Evangelicis, sic etiam ab eorum præcipuis quibusdam Ministris traditur: Adamum ante peccatum fuisse natura immortalem, post peccatum vero mortalem factum.
units.tr: Awelsingius, De Offic. hom. Christi., p. E.2. We make this first error: just as it is commonly taught by evangelicals, so also by certain of their chief ministers, that Adam before sin was immortal by nature, but after sin was made mortal.

units.la: Ibidem. Quod etiam ante peccatum Adamus mortalis, & quidem talis a Deo creatus fuerit, multa aperte docent.
units.tr: Ibid. Many things clearly teach that Adam was mortal before sin, and indeed was created by God as such.

units.la: Ibidem. pag.E.3. Si naturalem mortalitatem homini peccatum attulisset, esset que ea propria peccati pœna, certe eam Christus, qui peccatum, hoc est, peccati pœnam sustulit, ipsam naturalem mortalitatem abstulisset: quod tamen non fecit.
units.tr: Ibid. p. E.3. If sin had brought natural mortality upon man, and this were the proper punishment of sin, then surely Christ, who took away sin, that is the punishment of sin, would have taken away natural mortality itself; which however he did not do.

units.la: III. Intellectum hominis non esse adeo corruptum, quin homo possit sine Spiritus S. illuminatione intelligere o-mnia, quæ in Scripturis ad salutem æternam consequendam, scitu, creditu, speratu, & factu necessaria traduntur.
units.tr: III. That the intellect of man is not so corrupted that man cannot, without the illumination of the Holy Spirit, understand all those things which the Scriptures hand down as necessary for attaining eternal salvation, to be known, believed, hoped for and done.

units.la: A SIM. EPISCOPIO, Disp. de perspic. S. Script. Thes. 1.
units.tr: FROM SIMON EPISCOPIUS, Disputation on the Perspicuity of Holy Scripture, Thesis 1.

units.la: Clara & aperta sensuum omnium, qui universis & singulis ad æternam salutem consequendam scitu, creditu, speratu, factu necessarij sunt, per Scripturam propositio, sine labore examinis, sine auxilio operosæ indaginis, immediata sua luce & evidentia, a quolibet, modo usu rationis & judicij polleat, intelligi & percipi potest.
units.tr: The clear and open proposition, through Scripture, of all those meanings which are necessary for everyone and anyone to know, believe, hope for and do in order to attain eternal salvation can be understood and grasped by anyone who has the use of reason and judgment, without the labour of examination or the help of laborious investigation, by its own immediate light and evidence.

units.la: Ibidem. Thes. 3. Legentes igitur & audientes, quibus perspicua Scriptura est, non eos tantum statuimus, qui peculiari quadam, & immediata luce interius collustrati sunt, aut qui sibi hujusmodi luce & judicio donati ac præditi soli videntur, sed omnes in universum, quicunque & qualescunque tandem esse possint, summæ, mediæ, infimæ sortis homines, in quibus vel dictamen naturalis rationis & judicij aut omnino obliteratum non est, aut saltem non enormiter vitiatum, vel in quibus supina aut voluntaria quædam negligentia, manifesta inadvertentia, præjudicata sententia, aut dedita malitia locum non habet.
units.tr: Ibidem. Thesis 3. We therefore hold that by readers and hearers to whom Scripture is perspicuous we mean not only those who have been illuminated inwardly by some special and immediate light, or who alone seem to themselves endowed and furnished with such light and judgment, but all people in general, whatever and of whatever kind they may be, men of the highest, middle or lowest rank, in whom the dictate of natural reason and judgment is either not wholly obliterated, or at least not grossly corrupted, and in whom no supine or wilful negligence, manifest inattention, prejudiced opinion or settled malice has a place.

units.la: Disp. priv. de perspic. S. Scrip. Thes. 3. Ad hanc intelligentiam (omnium eorum quæ creditu ad salutem necessaria in S. Scriptura traduntur) consequendam, aliud necessarium non est, quam vis apprehendendi & percipiendi sensum illorum verborum, quæ clare & significanter proponuntur: quæ vis naturalis est, & omnibus ratione præditis communis, in o-mni statu.
units.tr: Private disputation on the perspicuity of Holy Scripture, Thesis 3. For attaining this understanding (of all those things which are set out in Holy Scripture as necessary to be believed for salvation), nothing else is needed than the power of apprehending and perceiving the meaning of those words which are clearly and significantly set forth: which power is natural, and common to all who are endowed with reason, in every condition.

units.la: Ibidem. Unde nec aliud ullum supernaturale lumen potentiæ superinfusum, eamque elevans ad hanc intelligentiam eliciendam necessario requiritur.
units.tr: Ibidem. Hence no other supernatural light infused into the faculty, and raising it, is necessarily required for eliciting this understanding.

units.la: Disp. privat. 46. Corol. 1. An ulla actio Spiritus Sancti immediata in voluntatem aut mentem necessaria sit, aut in Scripturis promittatur, ad hoc ut quis credere possit verbo extrinsecus proposito? Negativam tuebimur.
units.tr: Private disputation 46, Corollary 1. Is any immediate action of the Holy Spirit upon the will or mind necessary, or is it promised in the Scriptures, in order that a man may be able to believe a word proposed to him from outside? We shall defend the negative.

units.la: IV. Voluntatem hominis irregeniti non esse servam peccati, sed liberam ad bonum & ad malum volendum.
units.tr: IV. The will of unregenerate man is not a slave of sin, but free to will good and evil.

units.la: A REMONSTRANTIBUS, Coll.Hag.pag.250. In voluntate non potuit ejusmodi infusio (sanctitatis) locum habere, ut quæ natura sua libera est ad volendum bonum vel malum.
units.tr: FROM THE REMONSTRANTS, Coll. Hag., p. 250. Such an infusion (of holiness) could not take place in the will, since by its nature it is free to will good or evil.

units.la: Ibidem. In morte spirituali non separantur proprie dona spiritualia ab humana voluntate.
units.tr: Ibidem. In spiritual death the spiritual gifts are not properly separated from the human will.

units.la: Ibidem. Libertas bene aut male agendi mansit in homine tanquam pars naturæ, cum quâ creatus fuit.
units.tr: Ibidem. The liberty of acting well or ill remained in man as a part of the nature with which he was created.

units.la: A WELSINGIO, De Offic.hom. Christ. sol.B. 3. Dogma illud Evangelicorum de servo arbitrio, quo docetur hominis arbitrium in iis, quæ ad salutem æternam pertinent, nullam prorsus libertatem habere, ejusmodi est, ut ipsum per se omnem Religionem & pietatem possundare possit[?].
units.tr: FROM WELSINGIUS, De Officiis hominis Christiani, fol. B. 3. That dogma of the Evangelicals concerning the enslaved will, by which it is taught that man's will has absolutely no freedom in those things which pertain to eternal salvation, is of such a kind that it can overthrow all religion and piety in itself[?].

units.la: Ab ADOL. VENATORE, Declar.pag.173. Non possum credere homines omnes ab utero matris, corpore & animâ esse vitiatos, in intellectu plane occæcatos, & voluntate ad malum necessario proclives: qui verum bonum non possint intelligere, aut nihil aliud facere quam malum.
units.tr: FROM ADOLF VENATOR, Declaration, p. 173. I cannot believe that all men from the mother's womb are corrupted in body and soul, utterly blinded in understanding, and necessarily inclined to evil in will, so that they cannot understand the true good or do anything but evil.

units.la: Ibidem.pag.174. Non possum credere hominem habere voluntatem, quæ tantum serva sit peccati.
units.tr: Ibidem, p. 174. I cannot believe that man has a will which is merely a slave of sin.

units.la: Ibidem. pag. 175. Non possum credere hominem nullas habere vires, quibus servari possit: neque cum impotentia aliquâ natum esse.
units.tr: Ibidem, p. 175. I cannot believe that man has no powers by which he can be saved, nor that he is born with any impotence.

units.la: V. Hominem irregenitum ex se esse idoneum ad bonum spirituale cogitandum, volendum, & faciendum.
units.tr: V. That unregenerate man is of himself fit to think, will and do spiritual good.

units.la: A REMONSTRANTIBUS, Coll. Hag.pag. 254. Præcedit itaque aliqua actio hominis ipsius vivificationem, agnitio scilicet mortis suæ, ejus dolor & deploratio, desiderium & votum liberationis, fames & sitis vitæ: quæ omnia, sed & alia plura, à Christo requiruntur in eo, quem vivificaturus & regeneraturus est.
units.tr: FROM THE REMONSTRANTS, Coll. Hag., p. 254. Therefore some action of the man himself precedes his quickening: namely, the recognition of his own death, his grief and lamentation, desire and wish for deliverance, hunger and thirst for life. All these, and many others besides, are required by Christ in the one whom he is about to quicken and regenerate.

units.la: Ibidem.pag.251. Non omnes irregeniti sunt ejusdem ordinis, quidam sunt positi extra omnem vocationem: alii jam sunt vocati. Priores in Scripturis proprie vocantur mortui in peccatis: Posteriores vero isti mortui profecto non sunt.
units.tr: Ibidem, p. 251. Not all unregenerate are in the same condition: some are placed outside every calling, others have already been called. The former are properly called in Scripture dead in sins; but the latter are certainly not dead.

units.la: A WELSINGIO, De Offic. hom. Christ. Fol. B. 4. Nunquam verum esse ostendent Evangelici humanas vires in vitandis peccatis nullas esse: & propter primi hominis peccatum atque inobedientiam, universum humanum genus, ipsius voluntatis libertate in bene agendo; Deoque obediendo privatum esse.
units.tr: FROM WELSINGIUS, De Officiis hominis Christiani, fol. B. 4. The Evangelicals will never be shown to be right in holding that human powers for avoiding sin are nothing, and that because of the sin and disobedience of the first man the whole human race has been deprived of freedom of its own will in doing good, and of obeying God.

units.la: A VENATORE, Declar. pag. 174. Non possum credere hominem in illam impotentiam incidisse, ut non possit clamare, orare, desiderare, supplicare, quaerere, se praeparare, aut vocatum sequi: Neque possit bonum aliquod magnum aut parvum facere, quod Deo placeat, ut eo Deus moveatur ad majorem ei gratiam conferendam.
units.tr: FROM VENATOR, Declaration, p. 174. I cannot believe that man has fallen into such impotence that he cannot cry out, pray, desire, supplicate, seek, prepare himself, or follow when called; nor that he can do no good thing, great or small, that pleases God, so that God is moved by it to confer greater grace upon him.

units.la: VI. Gratiam DEI, quâ in homine DEUS operatur, quum intendit eum convertere, non operari in homine ipsum velle seu voluntatis assensum, neque solam, neque ita efficaciter, ut effectus semper consequatur, sed tali tantum modo, ut hic assensus semper relinquatur libero hominis arbitrio, atq; ab eodem pendeat: adeo ut DEUS gratia hac conversionis in multis operetur cum intentione eos convertendi, qui tamen nunquam convertantur. Ac proinde conversionis nostra causam efficientem non esse solam hanc DEI gratiam, sed liberum quoque voluntatis humanae arbitrium DEO cooperari, & conversionis nostrae causam esse partialem.
units.tr: VI. The grace of God, by which God works in man when he intends to convert him, does not itself work in man the willing, or the assent of the will, neither alone nor so effectively that the effect always follows, but only in such a way that this assent is always left to man's free choice and depends upon it; so that God, by this grace of conversion, works in many with the intention of converting them, who nevertheless are never converted. And therefore the efficient cause of our conversion is not this grace of God alone, but also the free choice of the human will cooperating with God, and the cause of our conversion is partial.

units.la: A REMONSTRANTIBUS, Coll. Hag. pag. 230. Agnoscimus quidem irresistibilem quandam vim Spiritus in intellectu, quum DEUS intellectum illuminans, voluntatem suam patefacit: & in corde, quando is corda nostra pulsat, sed gratia ea, qua voluntas nostra ad bonum determinatur, & Spiritus Sanctus in nobis actum fidei efficit, tocumque opus obedientiæ, quam ànobis DEUS in Euangelio exigit: hanc gratiam vocamus resistibilem, quia illi homo suâ voluntate potest resistere, & ejusactum impedire.
units.tr: FROM THE REMONSTRANTS, Coll. Hag., p. 230.
